Lucius Ferraris was an eighteenth-century Franciscan canonist, born at Solero near Alessandria, whose birth and death dates are unknown, though he seems to have died before 1763. Professor, provincial of his order, and consultor of the Holy Office, he built a working library for priests.

His Prompta Bibliotheca, an encyclopedia of canon, civil, moral, and theological knowledge, first appeared at Bologna in 1746. He enlarged it twice himself, and a posthumous fourth edition of 1763 added his notes and other hands' additions in place. Benedictine, Migne, Paris, and Rome editions kept it current, and it remains a mine of information, though critics charge its author with laxism at times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lycopolis:
Lycopolis is a titular see in Thebais Prima, suffragan of Antinoe, known today as Siout or Siaout. After the sixth dynasty fell, its princes swung between Heracleopolis and Thebes, and its chief god was the jackal Apouaitou, whence the Greek name, city of the wolf.

Its ancient bishops include Alexander, who wrote against the Manichaeans, Meletius, author of the Egyptian schism, and Volusianus, at Nicaea in 325. Theodosius threatened to raze the town after a fratricidal war, but St. John of Lycopolis saved it. Plotinus was born here, and under the Arabs it thrived as capital of Said and caravan rendezvous for Darfur, with a slave market, bazaar, and ancient necropolis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mactaris:
Mactaris is a titular see of the Byzantine Empire, now the village of Mactar, civil headquarters between Kairouan and the Kef in Tunisia, 950 metres above sea level in a well-watered land. No ancient geographer names it, but the Notitia Africae lists it among Byzantine towns.

Punic life long thrived here, shown by inscriptions, and it stayed a Roman town until at least 170, becoming a colony under Marcus Aurelius as Aelia Aurelia Mactaris. Enormous dolmens stand nearby, and the Roman ruins hold two triumphal arches, amphitheatre, baths, temple, aqueduct, and tombs. A basilica yielded Christian epitaphs, an altar over two martyrs, one named Felix, and six bishops from 255 to the sixth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcianopolis:
Marcianopolis was a titular see in Lower Moesia, on the Danube's right bank. Trajan named it for his sister Marciana, and it had earlier been called Parthenopolis. Claudius II beat back Goths near the town more than once. Valens wintered there in 368 and later years.

Avars sacked it in 587, and Romans retook it at once. A Roman army camped there in 596 before crossing the Danube against the Avars. Saints and martyrs crowd its story, from Meletina, honoured on 15 September, to Alexander, martyred under Maximianus. Maximus, Theodotus, and Asclepiodotus, born there, were martyred at Adrianople. Church lists give it five suffragans about 640 and confirm them about 840, but Leo the Wise and Constantine Porphyrogenitus omit it, since Bulgarians had overrun the region. Today it is Devna, west of Varna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcopolis:
Marcopolis was a titular see of Asia Minor, under Edessa. Its native name is unknown. It owes its Greek name to Emperor Marcus Aurelius. George of Cyprus describes it at the start of the seventh century, and Antioch's lists of bishoprics name it as a see of Osrhoene in the sixth century.

Two early bishops stand on record. Cyrus attended the Council of Ephesus in 431. Caioumas attended the Council of Chalcedon in 451. Eubel adds four more titular bishops between 1340 and 1400, plus a fifth from 1441 to 1453. Despite those names, the city's site has never been found. It survives only in geographers, council lists, and later titular rolls, a name without a place on the map.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-ferdin:
Martin Ferdinand Morris was a lawyer and jurist, born at Washington, D.C., in 1834 and dead there in 1909. From an Irish Catholic family, he graduated Georgetown in 1854 and entered the Jesuit novitiate at Frederick, Maryland, aiming for priesthood. His father's death left him sole support of mother and sisters, so that calling went unrealised.

He began law practice at Baltimore in 1863, moved to Washington in 1867, and partnered first with Richard T. Merrick, then, after Merrick died in 1885, with George E. Hamilton. He handled weighty cases in local courts and the Supreme Court until President Cleveland named him associate justice of the District of Columbia Court of Appeals at its founding in 1893. He helped found Georgetown Law School in 1871 and won its LL.D. in 1877. He wrote Lectures on the History of the Development of Constitutional and Civil Liberty, with many monographs and addresses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martyropolis:
Martyropolis was a titular see, suffragan of Amida in Mesopotamia or Armenia Quarta. It was only a small town named Maipherqat, but Bishop St Maruthas made it famous late in the fourth century. Enjoying great sway at Roman and Persian courts, Maruthas won religious liberty for Persian Christians in 410 through missions to Seleucia-Ctesiphon and Constantinople.

Returning from Persia with many martyrs' relics, he gave the town its new name, Martyropolis. Emperor Theodosius II aided his rebuilding and embellishment. Persians under Anastasius I seized it, Romans retook it, and Justinian's age saw it defended with success, briefly renamed Justinianopolis. It figures often in Roman-Persian wars from 584 to 589, Heraclius halted there in 624, and Arabs held it in 712. Now called Mefarkin or Silvan, 42 miles north-east of Diarbekir, it holds 7,000 people, with three churches for its faiths.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-de-sales:
Mary de Sales Chappuis, born Marie-Therese Chappuis, belonged to the Order of the Visitation of Holy Mary. She was born at Soyhieres in the Bernese Jura, then French territory, in 1793 and died at Troyes in 1875. Her father served in the French king's Cent-Suisses Guard, her mother was sister of Soyhieres's cure, and six of their eleven children entered religion.

She is chiefly famed for spreading a spirituality she called The Way, La Voie. Her director and biographer Father Brisson defined it as depending on God's actual will, relishing whatever pleased him, and imitating the Saviour's outward life. For years controversy has attended the Way's doctrinal worth, and disciples exaggerated the 1892 approbation of her writings, which was not absolute and left room for respectful criticism. Her life remains a study in Visitation spirituality and its limits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthew-paris:
St. Albans monk Matthew Paris (about 1200-1259) ranks first among English medieval chroniclers. He took the habit on 21 January 1217 and stayed at St. Albans for life. Yet he travelled to London and the court, and spent nearly a year as visitor to St. Benet Holm in Norway. He carried letters from St. Louis of France to King Haakon IV, won Haakon's friendship, and stood close to Henry III and Richard of Cornwall.

From court talk he gathered a wide, if not always exact, grasp of foreign affairs unmatched among his peers. His own hand likely drew the lively margin sketches in his manuscripts. His Chronica Majora runs from Creation to 1259. To 1235 it reworks Roger of Wendover with a patriotic, anti-papal slant, while from 1235 onward Paris speaks as a first-hand witness and the fullest source for the age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maximianopoli:
Maximianopolis, a titular see of Palestina Secunda under Scythopolis, began as Adad-Remmon, or Hadad-Rimmon in Hebrew. The name appears in Zechariah 12:11, likening Jerusalem's grief to the lament at Adadremmon on the plain of Megiddo, where Pharaoh Necho killed King Josiah. By the days of the Pilgrim of Bordeaux and St. Jerome, the place already bore the name Maximianopolis.

Three ancient bishops are known: Paul in 325, not Maximus as Le Quien prints, Megas in 518, and Domnus in 536. The town has since resumed its old name of Rimmon. It survives as the nearly deserted village of Roum-meneh, about four miles south of Ledjun, the ancient Legio. The entry corrects Le Quien's error on Paul's name and points readers to Guerin, Gelzer, and Legendre for the site's description.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maximopolis:
Maximopolis, a titular see of Arabia under Bostra, owes its name to a mix-up worth untangling. Its true name is Maximianopolis, as shown in the sixth-century Notitia episcopatuum of Patriarch Anastasius. A Propaganda decree of 1885 ordered the title suppressed, since Torquato Amellini had confused this town with Maximianopolis in Palestina Secunda. Its last titular was consecrated in 1876.

Two ancient bishops are known: Severus, who signed at Chalcedon in 451, and Peter, known from an inscription. The earlier name of the place is unknown, and its site is not certain. Many place it at Sheikh-Miskin in the Hauran, a spot famed for wide and lovely ruins, where an inscription bearing the name of Bishop Thomas has been found. The entry is a brief lesson in how one scholar's confusion can create a phantom see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-meletius-of-l:
Meletius of Lycopolis in Egypt gave his name to a schism of short life. The dates of his birth, death, and episcopate are uncertain, but he was bishop of that city by 303. In a council about 306 at Alexandria, Peter, archbishop of that city, deposed him for several reasons, among them sacrificing to idols. Athanasius's scant references were our only source until the eighteenth century, when Scipio Maffei found documents at Verona on the Meletian schism.

Three Latin documents survive and are surely authentic. First comes a protest letter from four Egyptian bishops, Hesychius, Pachomius, Theodore, and Phileas, dating at latest from 307, from the schism's very start and before Meletius's excommunication. They call him beloved fellow minister in the Lord, yet report grievous charges. He troubled divine law and church rules, and, against ancient law, ordained outside his own diocese without regard for the great bishop of Alexandria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-memphis:
Memphis, ancient capital of Egypt and a diocese of Arcadia, or Heptanomos, under Oxyrynchus, bore many Egyptian names. It was called Mennophir, the good place, a name first kept for Pharaoh Pepi I's pyramid, then spread to the quarter and the whole city. Other names include Aneb, city of the wall, and Aneb-hadj, the white wall, for the citadel.

Ha-ka-Ptah, dwelling of Ptah's person, was first the temple's name, then the city's, and by some accounts the root of the Greek Aiguptos, Egypt. Menes, a native of Thini, is held to have founded Memphis, which served as capital of several dynasties: the third, fourth, sixth, eighth, and twenty-fourth. After Thebes, says Brugsch, no city teaches more through monuments and papyri. The Bible names it Mof or Nof, and the prophets foretold its ruin in strong terms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-metellopolis:
Metellopolis, a titular see of Phrygia Pacatiana in Asia Minor, began as the Phrygian town Motella. Inscriptions link Motella with the Phrygian woman's name Motalis, the Cilician man's name Motales, and Mutalli, an ancient Hittite king of northern Commagene. One inscription found at Medele, in the vilayet of Broussa, plainly preserves the old name. Motella seems to be the town Hierocles calls Pulcherianopolis, perhaps raised to a bishopric by Empress Pulcheria.

Shortly before 553, perhaps in 535, Justinian raised Hierapolis to metropolitan rank and attached suffragans formerly under Laodicea. Among them the Notitiae Episcopatuum name this same Motella, called Metellopolis, and once Metallopolis, from the ninth to the twelfth or thirteenth century. Inscriptions name Bishop Michael in 556 and Bishop Cyriacus, perhaps in 667. Eudoxius, priest and monk, represented the see at Nicaea in 787, and Bishop Michael attended Constantinople's councils in 869 and 879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-metempsychosi:
Metempsychosis, from Greek meta empsychos, is the doctrine of the transmigration of souls: the same soul dwells in turn in the bodies of different beings, men and animals alike. It was held by many systems of thought and faith far apart in place and time. Today civilized peoples link it almost solely with Asia, above all India. Yet at one time or another it has flourished nearly everywhere, and it still prevails in varied forms among peoples across the globe.

That spread marks it as a spontaneous, instinctive answer to existence's deep and urgent problems. Its many rich and varied forms, and the bright mythology clothing it, show a belief that grips the imagination and bends with ease to widely different minds. Its success seems to rest partly on a basic faith in immortality, and partly on its sweep, binding all single lives into one unbroken scheme.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-miletopolis:
Miletopolis, a titular see of Asia Minor and suffragan of Cyzicus, was a town north of Mysia at the meeting of the Macestus and Rhyndacus rivers, west of Lake Miletopolitis. A tribe called the Milatae lived there, and Miletopolis was their chief town, its name Hellenized to suggest a colony from Miletus.

Almost nothing is known of Miletopolis's history except that its people helped colonize the city of Gargara. It has been identified with Bali-Kesser, Manias, and Mikhalitch, but the first two identifications are certainly wrong and the third doubtful. It more probably stood at Hammamli in the vilayet of Brusa, where remains of an ancient town have been found.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montes-pietat:
Montes pietatis were charitable credit institutions that lent money at low or no interest against objects left in pawn. They shielded people in want from usurers. They served only those facing a genuine crisis, such as famine or misfortune. Any surplus went toward wages and wider charitable work rather than profit.

The word mons, meaning heap or fund, already described public debts at Venice, Genoa and Florence centuries earlier. Grain and flour montes once joined the money kind. The entry traces the pawnshops from their Franciscan founding in fifteenth-century Italy. It covers debates over whether charging interest was usury, their spread across Europe, and their rules for pledges, sales and the care of the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mosynoupolis:
Mosynoupolis was a titular see in Rhodope, suffragan to Trajanopolis, whose history survives in scattered mentions rather than a full record. Only one bishop is known, Paul, who attended the council of 878 that restored Photius.

The see appears in the Notitia of Leo the Wise about 900, again in 940, and in 1170 under the name Misinoupolis. The monk Ephrem records that Emperor Frederick of Swabia captured the city in 1190 and that Calojan, Tsar of the Bulgarians, ravaged it about 1206. Where exactly this Macedonian town stood, and what name it bears today, is not known.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neocaesarea-h:
Neocaesarea in Hierapolis was a titular see, suffragan of Hierapolis in the Patriarchate of Antioch, sometimes called Caesarea. Among its bishops were Paul, whose hands were burned by order of Licinius and who attended Nicaea in 325. Meletius, opposed to the Council of Ephesus in 431, Patricius in 451 and John in 553 also served.

The sixth-century Notitia of Anastasius lists it as a suffragan of Hierapolis. Procopius records that Justinian accomplished great things there. Neocaesarea was a fort on the Euphrates, not far from Zeugma. Chabot places its site at the actual ruins of Balkiz. The entry is brief, resting on Le Quien, Gelzer and Chabot, and it leaves the fort's full history to the larger sees around it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-d-orb:
Nicolas d'Orbellis, a Franciscan thinker of the fifteenth century, taught the philosophy of John Duns Scotus at Angers. Born around 1400, he joined the Observant Franciscans and won a name as a clear expounder of Scotus, whose subtle teaching earned its master the title of Subtle Doctor.

After 1465 he wrote his principal work, a commentary on the Sentences in four books, printed many times across Europe. Commentaries on Aristotle's Metaphysics and on logic, plus a short work on mathematics, complete a career that ended at Rome in 1475. He was buried in the church of Ara Coeli on the Capitoline at Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolaus-von-:
Bishop Nicolaus von Weis of Speyer, born in Lorraine in 1796, built Catholic publishing and schooling in nineteenth-century Germany. Ordained in 1818 after study at Mainz, he taught, served parishes, and rose through the Speyer cathedral chapter while writing and translating constantly.

With Andreas Räss he enlarged Butler's Lives of the Saints into twenty-four German volumes and founded the monthly Der Katholik in 1821, editing it alone for fourteen years. Named bishop in 1842, he promoted missions, retreats, and Christian education until his death in 1869. He promoted popular missions, pious societies, and annual retreats for priests in his diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicopolis:
Nicopolis on the Danube, built by Trajan to mark his victory over the Dacians, anchors this Bulgarian diocesan entry. Placed by Ptolemy in Thrace and by Hierocles in Moesia, it stood as an autocephalous archbishopric around 640, then vanished from episcopal lists under Bulgarian rule.

The city is best remembered for 25 September 1396, when French and Hungarian armies fell to the Turks and left them masters of the Balkans. Later Franciscans, Baptistines, and Passionists carried the Latin mission there, and the entry lists its bishops and modern parishes. Two ancient bishops survive in the record, Marcellus in 458 and Amantius in 518.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nilopolis:
Nilopolis, an Egyptian titular see on a Nile island in the Heraclean nome, survives today as Delas near Beni Suef. Ptolemy places it on the river, Eusebius names its bishop Cheremon under the Decian persecution, and John of Nikiu mentions it during the Muslim conquest.

By the fourteenth century the town paid 20,000 dinars in taxes, a mark of real weight. Modern Delas, on the Nile's left bank about forty-seven miles from Memphis, holds some 2,500 people, nearly a thousand of them nomadic Bedouin. John of Nikiu mentions the city in connection with the Muslim occupation of Egypt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nisibis:
Nisibis, a Mesopotamian city on the Mygdonius below Mount Masius, changed hands between Rome and Persia for centuries. Greeks called it Antiochia Mygdonia, Lucullus and Trajan took it, Septimius Severus made it his base, and Rome ceded it to Persia in 363 after Julian's defeat.

Its see, founded in 300, grew into the metropolis of Beit-Arbaye with six suffragans by 410, and its school trained theologians of the Church of the East. Saint James defended the city by prayer during Sapor's sieges, and the entry follows its bishops into later centuries. In 410 it already counted six suffragan sees under its metropolitan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nunc-dimittis:
The Nunc Dimittis, Simeon's canticle in Luke's Gospel, closes the three great Evangelical Canticles after the Magnificat and Benedictus. Its title comes from the Vulgate’s opening words, in which Simeon asks the Lord to dismiss his servant, spoken when the aged Simeon held the Christ child in the Temple.

Promised he would not die before seeing the Lord's Christ, Simeon sang of salvation prepared before all peoples, a light for Gentiles and glory for Israel. The entry traces its echoes of Isaiah and the Psalms and its place in evening prayer and the Apostolic Constitutions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ordericus-vit:
Anglo-Norman historian Ordericus Vitalis, born in 1075, spent his life as a monk of Saint-Évroult while writing a history of his age. His mother was English; his father, a French priest, came with the Normans, and he crossed to Normandy at ten and stayed at Saint-Évroult, traveling to Cambrai, Cluny, and England.

Calling himself Vitalis the Englishman, he turned an abbey chronicle into a thirteen-book Ecclesiastical History, from the Christian era to 1143, with Norman conquests, his abbey's story, and the First Crusade. Chronologically tangled and often inaccurate, it stays discriminating in sources and wide in sympathy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ostiensis:
Ostiensis was the surname of Leo Marsicanus, a Benedictine chronicler born about 1045 and dead on 22 May 1115, 1116, or 1117. Of old noble stock, he entered Monte Cassino at fourteen and won the regard of Abbot Desiderius, later Pope Victor III. Desiderius gave his schooling to the future Cardinal Aldemar, and Leo became librarian and archivist of the house.

His chief task was settling land disputes from the monastery's papers. Abbot Oderisius pressed him to write the house history, but his many duties kept him from giving it full time. Paschal II made him Cardinal Bishop of Ostia, and he defended the papacy stoutly against Henry V. His unfinished chronicle, covering 529 to 1075 and continued by Peter the Deacon to 1139, stays a trusted mine of detail for southern Italian history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paleopolis:
Paleopolis, or Old City, was a titular see of Asia Minor under Ephesus, and its history is unknown. Hierocles names it in the sixth century, and bishop lists carry it as late as the thirteenth century among Ephesus's suffragans. Today it is the town of Baliambol in the Smyrna region.

Le Quien names seven of its bishops, known only by their presence at councils. Rhodon sat at Ephesus in 431, Basilicus at Chalcedon in 451, and Eusebius at Constantinople in 536. George sat at Constantinople in 692, Gregory at Nicaea in 787, Peter at Constantinople in 869, and Julian at Constantinople in 879. No other deeds of the see survive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-panopolis:
Panopolis was a titular see, suffragan of Antinoe in Thebais Prima, the ancient Apu or Khimmin, which Greeks called Khemmis and Panopolis. It served as capital of its district and ranked among Upper Egypt's chief towns, famed for its god Min. Herodotus notes its temple, and Strabo says its people were weavers and stone-cutters.

Le Quien names bishops Arius, friend of Saint Pachomius, who built three convents there, Sabinus at Ephesus in 431, Saint Menas, honoured on 11 February, and later Jacobites. Recent digs bared a necropolis, Coptic tapestries akin to Gobelin work from the second to ninth centuries, Christian manuscripts including Enoch fragments and Peter's Gospel and Apocalypse, and many inscriptions. The town is now Akhmin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paris:
Paris is an archdiocese covering the Department of the Seine, remade by the Concordat of 1802 within far narrower bounds than before the Revolution. Old Paris had held the Josas and Brie archdeaconries, with 492 parishes. Versailles and Meaux took those lands, leaving Paris 42 urban and 76 suburban parishes. It first held eight suffragans, later trimmed when Reims, Sens, and Cambrai rose as metropolitans.

Roman Lutetia, burnt by Camulogenus in 52 before Christ, rose again as capital of the Parisii tribe. It grew into the French capital's church heart. Later pages tour its parishes and martyred pastors, Le Ber in 1792 and Deguerry in 1871. They cover churches from Saint Lawrence to Saint Lazare, and orders from the Sisters of Charity to the Sacred Heart sisters, with schools, hospitals, and missions across the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paris-de-gras:
Paris de Grassis was master of ceremonies to Julius II and Leo X, born at Bologna about 1470 and dead at Rome on 10 June 1528. Nephew of Antonio de Grassis, nuncio to Frederick III and Bishop of Tivoli, and brother of Cardinal Achille de Grassis, he succeeded the famed Burchard in 1506 and carried on his diary. His portion covers Julius II's closing years and Leo X's pontificate.

De Grassis was no historian, only a chronicler, noting with pedantic faithfulness every ceremony, curial trifle, consistory, procession, ambassador's coming and going, and journey. He held no political slant, though he liked France and some curial figures little, and cared only for ceremony and court etiquette. Yet his sharp eye caught anecdotes that light up both popes, and his journeys beside Julius, as in the Romagna campaign, fill gaps in larger histories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parlais:
Parlais was a titular see of Pisidia, suffragan of Antioch, called Julia Augusta Parlais as a Roman colony. Coins were struck under that title. Ptolemy calls it Paralais and places it in Lycaonia. Kiepert identifies it with Barla in the Koniah region, while Ramsay puts it among ruins known as Uzumla Monastir.

Bishop lists name the see as late as the thirteenth century, as Parlaos, Paralaos, and even Parallos. Four bishops are known: Patricius at Constantinople in 381, Libanius at Chalcedon in 451, George at Constantinople in 692, and Anthimus at Constantinople in 879. Academius, who sat at Nicaea in 325, belonged to Pappa, not Parlais, despite Le Quien's claim.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paroecopolis:
Paroecopolis was a titular see of Macedonia, suffragan of Thessalonica, placed by Ptolemy in Sintice. Hierocles and Constantine Porphyrogenitus call it Parthicopolis, though the latter puts it in Thrace, and Stephanus Byzantius calls it Parthenopolis. Stephanus, after Theagenes, tells its founding legend: Geraestus, son of Mygdon, named it for his two daughters. Pliny uses the same name, also in Thrace.

Its bishop Jonas, or John, attended Sardica in 342 or 343, and at Chalcedon in 451 sat John of Parthicopolis in First Macedonia. No Greek bishop list mentions the see. Beyond its tangled names and two bishops at Sardica and Chalcedon, little more of the see is known.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parsis:
The Parsis are a small Indian community of Zoroastrians, emigrants from Persia. The 1881 census counted 85,397 in India, plus about 3,000 elsewhere and 8,000 in Persia, for a world total under 100,000. Of India's Parsis, 82,091 lived in the Bombay presidency, over half in Bombay City itself, with Surat, Broach, and Gujarat sharing the rest. By 1901 India held 94,190.

Persian Zoroastrians, called Iranis, cluster at Yezd and its twenty-four villages, with about 1,000 families counted in 1854, plus Kerman and Tehran groups. Once far more numerous, they now steadily decline. Later pages trace their flight from Muslim Persia, their landing in Gujarat, their fire temples and towers of silence, their trade wealth in Bombay, and their customs, marriage rules, and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-atkinson:
Paul Atkinson of Saint Francis was a notable confessor of the English Church in the age after bloody persecution. Condemned to lifelong imprisonment for his priesthood about 1699, he died in confinement after bearing it over thirty years. Of a Yorkshire family and baptised Matthew, he joined the English Franciscan convent at Douai in 1673.

He spent twelve years on the English mission, winning distinction there before a maidservant betrayed him for the 100-pound reward. One governor of Hurst Castle on the Solent let him walk outside the prison wall, but complaint ended that leave. His long captivity replaced martyrdom by the sword, and his name stands among England's steadfast confessors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-godet-de:
Paul Godet des Marais was Bishop of Chartres, born at Talcy near Blois in 1647 and dead at Chartres in 1709. He studied at Saint-Sulpice, took his theology doctorate at the Sorbonne, was ordained, and in 1677 became superior of the Seminary of the Thirty-Three. Louis XIV named him to Chartres in 1690, but French-Holy See strains delayed papal confirmation until 21 January 1692.

As spiritual director of Madame de Maintenon, for whom he wrote Letters of Direction, he used his sway to remove Madame Guyon from Saint-Cyr. A staunch foe of Quietism, he joined Noailles and Bossuet in the 1697 Declaration condemning Fenelon's Maxims of the Saints. In 1698 he wrote pastoral letters against the pseudo-mysticism of Molinos, Fenelon, and Guyon. He fought Jansenism, refuted the case of conscience in 1703, and enforced Clement XI's constitution in 1705.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pentapolis:
Pentapolis was the name for the five cities of the lower Jordan Valley: Sodom, Gomorrha, Zoar, Adama, and Seboim. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry places them in the fertile Kikkar, the plain around the Dead Sea where Lot settled. It retells their league against the eastern kings, their defeat in the Valley of Siddim, their revolt twelve years later, and Abraham's rescue of the captive Lot.

Prosperity returned, and with it the vices that drew divine judgment. Four of the five cities were destroyed by brimstone and fire, while Zoar alone escaped. The entry weighs the geography of the Kikkar and identifies the invading kings with figures like Hammurabi and Kudur-Lagamar. It follows the region's place in Genesis from the patriarchal stories to the ruin of the plain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-cellens:
Peter Cellensis was a twelfth-century Benedictine abbot and Bishop of Chartres, born of noble Champagne stock. Schooled at St. Martin-des-Champs in Paris, he became abbot of La Celle near Troyes in 1150, taking his surname from the house, then abbot of St. Rémy at Reims in 1162. In 1181 he succeeded John of Salisbury as Bishop of Chartres, dying there on 20 February 1183.

Men of weight esteemed him, from Becket and Archbishop Eskil to Popes Eugene III and Alexander III. His writings, edited in 1671 and reprinted in the Patrologia, run to 177 letters, 95 sermons, and four treatises. The letters carry real historical value, while the sermons and treatises, on the loaves, the tabernacle, conscience, and cloister discipline, are notably ornate and allegorical.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-de-bloi:
Peter of Blois was a twelfth-century statesman, diplomat, and theologian, born about 1130. He studied at Tours, law at Bologna, and theology at Paris, where he taught the liberal arts. In 1167 Count Stephen du Perche carried him to Sicily as tutor to the king, keeper of the royal seal, and counsellor to the queen. Jealous nobles drove the foreign favourite out within two years.

England gave him his second career. He served Henry II as a diplomatic agent to pope and French king, became chancellor to Canterbury's archbishop and Archdeacon of Bath in 1176, and carried missions to Rome and Verona. After Henry's death he fell from favour, called Richard the Lionheart a new Pharaoh, and served Queen Eleanor as secretary. Archdeacon of London at the last, he died about 1203, poor beside his former power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-de-hone:
Peter de Honestis was a Ravenna nobleman turned founder, born about 1049 and descended from St. Romuald of the Camaldolese. All his life he fasted every Saturday for Our Lady and urged the practice on his monks, styling himself Peter the Sinner. Years in the Holy Land ended with a storm-tossed Adriatic crossing, on which he vowed to build a church to Our Lady if he reached harbour safely.

He kept the vow on family land, joined a small community of clerics nearby, and became their superior when they moved into his new church and monastery in 1099. His name links to the Children of Mary sodality and the Madonna Greca picture, said to come from Constantinople. Statutes he drew from St. Augustine's rule, approved by Paschal II, grew into the Portuensis Congregation. He died on 29 March 1119.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petropolis:
Petropolis was a Brazilian diocese in Rio de Janeiro state, erected in 1895. Its see began at Nictheroy under Leo XIII in 1893, moved to Petropolis in 1895, and returned to Nictheroy in 1908. Petropolis itself was founded by Brazil's emperor in 1845 as a German immigrant colony named for Dom Pedro, a pleasant summer resort that served as state capital in 1894.

Nictheroy, on Rio's bay, had been the provincial capital from 1834 until 1894, when Rio city became a neutral municipality. The entry names three bishops: François de Rogo Maia, elected in 1893, Jean-François Braga, transferred to Curitiba in 1907, and Augustin-François Bennassi, elected in 1908. Statistics count 15,548 square miles, over a million Catholics, 123 parishes, and 124 priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-phaselis:
Phaselis was a Dorian trading city on the Pamphylian Gulf, set on an isthmus between two harbours. That fortunate site made it a commercial crossroads for Greece, Asia, Egypt, and Phoenicia, outside the Lycian confederation. It drew the city into alliance with Cilician pirates, first by trade and then by treaty. When Servilius took Olympus and besieged Phaselis, its defender Zenicetus fired the city and leapt into the flames with his companions.

Recovery followed, but the little harbour silted into a pestilential swamp, and the city decayed completely. Its temple of Athena displayed the lance of Achilles, it gave birth to the poet Theodectes, its roses yielded a prized essence, and its coin bore the phaselos bark it invented. Two bishops are known, Fronto at Chalcedon and Aristodemus in 458, and its ruins lie at Tekir Ova.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-michae:
Philip Michael Ellis was an English Benedictine bishop, born in 1652 to an Anglican rector's family of divided loyalties. Of six brothers, John served William III, William served the exiled James II, Welbore became a Protestant bishop in Ireland, and Philip turned Catholic as a Westminster schoolboy. At eighteen he went to St. Gregory's, Douai, and professed as Michael in 1670.

Ordained, he returned to the English mission in 1685 as a royal chaplain, and in 1688 became first Vicar Apostolic of the Western District. The Revolution imprisoned him briefly, then drove him to St. Germain and Rome, where his knowledge of English affairs kept him from returning despite repeated pleas. Resigning the vicariate in 1704, he became Bishop of Segni in 1708, rebuilding St. Chiara's monastery as his seminary. He died in 1726.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippopolis:
Philippopolis was a titular see in Arabia, suffragan to Bostra, founded by Emperor Philip the Arabian, who reigned from 244 to 249. Aurelius Victor records that Philip built the town and gave it his name. It grew fast, as fine ruins at Shohba in the Hauran still prove, colonnades of a temple and colossal baths among them. Its ancient name before Philip is unknown.

As a see it appears in the episcopal lists of the sixth century. Bishop Hormisdas attended Chalcedon in 451, and an inscription names a Bishop Basil in 553. Later centuries added titular bishops of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. This short Catholic Encyclopedia entry gathers the town's founding, its ruins, and its bishops in a few lines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-sylvai:
Pierre Sylvain Régis was a French philosopher who spread the ideas of Descartes across southern France. Descartes was the thinker who grounded knowledge in reason. Régis was born near Agen in 1632 and studied under Rohault at the Sorbonne. He became a keen Cartesian and taught the system with great success at Toulouse, Montpellier, and Paris.

A ban on teaching Cartesianism ended his lectures. His three-volume Complete Course of Philosophy of 1690 set out Descartes in orderly form, softened toward experience. He denied that the soul holds inborn eternal ideas. He also answered Malebranche's idealism in journal articles and joined the Academy of Sciences in 1699, dying in Paris in 1707.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pompeiopolis:
Pompeiopolis, a titular see of Paphlagonia, stands today as Tach-Keupru, the bridge of stone, twenty-five miles northeast of Kastamouni. Its old name is lost; Eupatoria is a guess. Pompey placed it, with Andrapa-Neapolis, in the Province of Pontus in 64 BC, an annexation made too soon. As a metropolis the town went back to vassal princes of eastern Paphlagonia, then passed to Rome for good in 6 BC.

Strabo records a realgar mine close by, sulphuret of arsenic, dug by criminals. Mid-seventh century, the Ecthesis counted Pompeiopolis an autocephalous archdiocese; in the eleventh century it rose to metropolitan rank, holding it into the fourteenth before suppression. Le Quien lists fourteen titulars, the last Gregory near 1350, among them Philadelphus at Nicaea in 325 and John at Constantinople in 869.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-port-louis:
Port Louis diocese covers Mauritius, Rodriguez, Chagos, and Diego Garcia. Mauritius was found by the Portuguese about 1507 without settlement. The Dutch named it for Maurice of Nassau in 1598, colonized it in 1644, and left in 1710 or 1712. France renamed it Ile de France in 1715, made it the East's French government seat in 1789, and lost it to Britain in 1810, ceded formally in 1814. French language and law survived, and Britain restored the old name.

Port Louis, capital on the northwest coast, holds the Catholic and Anglican bishoprics and the governor's residence. The 1901 census counted 373,336 islanders, 113,244 of them Catholics, and 52,740 in Port Louis town. Catholics made up 64.71 per cent of school pupils in state-aided government and denominational schools. A prefecture apostolic for the Indian Ocean islands began in 1712 under the Vincentians. Benedict XIV tied the mission to Paris in 1740. After Britain took Mauritius, a vicariate apostolic followed, confirmed in January 1819.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ptolemais:
Ptolemais, the ancient name of Acre, now Saint-Jean d'Acre, was a titular metropolis in Phoenicia Prima. This encyclopedia entry explains that Ptolemy the Second, surnamed Philadelphus, renamed the city in 281 or 267 BC, and the new name lived on beside the old one as the official title. A Christian community stood there very early, visited by Saint Paul on his journey recorded in Acts. The see answered to Tyre as its suffragan.

Known bishops run from Clarus, present about 190 at a council on the Easter observance. Aeneas sat at Nicaea in 325 and Antioch in 341. Nectabus sat at Constantinople in 381. Antiochus, first friend then foe of Saint John Chrysostom, follows. Helladius, Paul, John and George carry the list to 553. Modern Acre closes the entry, with its hospital, boys' school, the Ladies of Nazareth school, and a Protestant school and hospital run by the Church Missionary Society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quicumque-chr:
Quicumque Christum Quaeritis opens the twelfth and last poem of Prudentius's Cathemerinon, a hymn for the Epiphany. This encyclopedia entry counts 52 strophes of iambic dimeter in that poem, 208 lines in all. An irregular pick from those lines has furnished four hymns to the Roman Breviary, each closing with the usual Marian doxology, Jesu tibi sit gloria. Prudentius did not write the doxology itself.

The four centos, or patchwork hymns, serve different feasts. Quicumque Christum quaeritis itself, sixteen lines drawn from three passages, serves Matins and both Vespers of the Transfiguration. Though written for Epiphany, its lines fit the Transfiguration well, as Daniel noted. Salvete flores martyrum, the hymn for the Holy Innocents, appears in ancient use in varied lengths and orders, with manuscript witnesses reaching back to the tenth century. The Roman Breviary follows Prudentius's own order, and official melodies for the hymns were in proof by 1911.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regulae-juris:
Regulae Juris, the Rules of Law, are general rules or principles used chiefly to interpret laws. In a narrower sense they are basic laws cast as short maxims in the Corpus Juris. Eleven were added by Gregory the Ninth at the end of the fifth Book of Decretals, and eighty-eight by Boniface the Eighth in the last title of the Liber Sextus. They sum up several laws on one subject as conclusions or deductions, rather than principles drawn from constitutions or court decisions.

Following Justinian's Digest, they stand in the last title of each book. Few general statements hold without exception, the entry warns: some maxims apply in every matter, others only in trials, benefices, and the like. As a sample it gives rule 47: nobody may use an agent to do what he cannot lawfully do himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhodiopolis:
Rhodiopolis was a titular see of Lycia, suffragan of Myra. Ptolemy and Stephanus Byzantius call it Rhodia, its coins and inscriptions say Rhodiapolis, and Pliny, calling it Rhodiopolis, places it in the mountains north of Corydalla. Its history is unknown.

Its ruins stand on a forested hill at Eski Hissar, in the vilayet of Koniah: churches, sarcophagi, a small theatre, an aqueduct, and a temple of Escalapius. Nicholas, present at Constantinople in 518, is the only bishop known, and the lists of sees mention Rhodiopolis as late as the twelfth or thirteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-cenali:
Robert Cenalis, also written Ceneau or Coenalis, was a French bishop, historian, and controversialist of the Reformation age. Born at Paris in 1483, he became a doctor of theology at the Sorbonne in 1513. He was made Bishop of Vence in 1515, transferred to Riez in 1530, and then to Avranches in 1532.

He threw himself into the religious disputes of his day, writing defences of clerical celibacy, on the two swords, on divorce, against Calvin, and on curbing heretics. His Historia Galliae of 1557, dedicated to Henry II, treated the name, origin, and deeds of Gauls, Franks, and Burgundians, though it has little critical value. While Bishop of Riez he issued synodal statutes and wrote a learned treatise on weights and measures. He died at Paris in 1560.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rule-of-saint:
St Francis founded three orders, each with a special rule; this entry treats the Friars Minor's rule. Much doubt surrounds the Rule: whether Francis wrote several rules or one in several versions, and whether its final form is his or others'. In many cases it is more a question of words than facts. Three successive rules are spoken of, of 1209, 1221, and 1223, chiefly the 1223 rule.

The 1209 rule, presented to Innocent III, has an unknown real text. From Thomas of Celano and St Bonaventure, it was little more than Gospel passages heard in 1208 in the Portiuncula chapel. Passages from Matthew and Luke, appearing in the second rule, are considered part of the original. They enjoin apostolic life with its renouncements and privations. The three vows of obedience, chastity, and poverty were added, with some practical rules of conduct.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacris-solemn:
Sacris solemniis are the opening words of the Matins hymn for Corpus Christi and the Votive Office of the Blessed Sacrament, composed by St Thomas Aquinas. Its rhythmic stanza imitates classical measures found in Horace and several Breviary hymns. Whatever it lacks in classical prosody, it compensates in an intricate rhymic scheme. The sixth stanza, sometimes used alone at Benediction, illustrates it. Panis angelicus, the Angelic Bread, feeds the sons of men.

Translators vary much on an apt English equivalent. The first words suggest English dactylics by tonic accents. The felicitous Anglican translator, Dr J.M. Neale, used iambic metre. His fifth stanza does not strictly follow the rhymic scheme, better observed in a Sursum Corda translation of 1908. Shipley's Annus Sanctus gives Wallace's translation in another form, and Caswall's Lyra Catholica gives a condensed translation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-denis:
Saint-Denis is a diocese erected in 1850 as suffragan of Bordeaux, including Reunion island, about 350 miles east of Madagascar. The island was discovered by the Portuguese in 1513, first called Sancta Appollonia, later Mascareigne. In 1638 France hoisted its flag there, and in 1642 Pronis took possession for France.

In 1646 twelve colonists were transported there, and in 1649 Flacourt renamed it Bourbon. From 1654 to 1658 Thaureau and thirteen others attempted colonization. In 1665 Governor Regnault arrived with the island's first colonists. The first apostles were Louis de Matos and Jourdie, a Lazarist there from 1667 to 1670. In 1674 Bernardin arrived, planted cotton, and governed from 1686 to 1689. In 1711 Clement XI entrusted the island to Lazarists. In 1848 the island took the name Reunion and slavery ended; the see followed two years later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-germain:
Germain of Paris, born near Autun about 496 and dead at Paris on 28 May 576, studied at Avalon and Luzy under his cousin Scapilion, a priest. Ordained at thirty-four, he became abbot of Saint-Symphorien near Autun. His alms-giving was so lavish that his monks, fearing he would give everything away, rebelled against him. Happening to be in Paris in 555 when Bishop Eusebius died, he was kept there by King Childebert and consecrated to the vacant see with the clergy and people agreeing.

Under his influence the worldly king reformed and lived a Christian life, while Germain pressed against pagan practices still lingering in Gaul and the excesses at Christian festivals. He attended the councils of Paris in 557 and 573 and of Tours in 566. From a relic of Saint Vincent brought back from Saragossa rose the suburban church later completed and dedicated by Germain on 23 December 588, the very day Childebert died.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-thais:
Thais, a fourth-century Egyptian penitent, is pictured burning her treasures or praying in a cell with a scroll begging mercy from her Creator. Two lives survive: an early Greek one, perhaps from the fifth century, and a verse life by Marbod, bishop of Rennes, who died in 1123. Her entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia treats her story as legend with a moral core.

Once a public sinner in Egypt, Thais was converted by the hermit Paphnutius, though some accounts name Bessarion or Serapion instead. Shut in a convent cell for three years of penance, she was then released among the nuns and lived only fourteen days more. The entry notes her name in Greek lists for 8 October, and leaves the question of the true hermit open.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salamis:
Salamis, a titular see in Cyprus, was a seaport on the island's eastern coast at the end of a fertile plain between two mountains, near the River Pediaeus. Already important by the sixth century before Christ, it claimed Teucer, son of Telamon, as founder, though others call it Phoenician and derive its name from a Semitic word for peace. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a city of kings and sieges.

A fine harbour and strong walls made it the island's chief city, ruled by kings allied with Cyrene. Gorgus refused the Ionian revolt and was expelled by his brother, then won his city back, and later kings fought Persia for a decade under Evagoras, praised by Isocrates. In 306 before Christ the greatest naval battle of the age was fought off Salamis, and the entry carries the story down to its Christian bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sanctorum-mer:
Sanctorum Meritis is the hymn for first and second Vespers in the Common of Martyrs in the Roman Breviary. Its authorship is often given to Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of Mainz, who died in 856, and both Blume and Dreves favour that ascription, praising his originality and poetic power. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia studies a hymn's metre as well as its words.

Each stanza, in classical measure, holds three Asclepiadic lines and one Glyconic. In Horace that stanza suggests grave thought, yet Breviary hymns in the same measure usually breathe triumphant joy, like the hymns for the Precious Blood, St Joseph, and Corpus Christi. Dom Johner classes such hymns among those where word accent rules and metrical beat shows only in places, above all in the fourth line.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scythopolis:
Scythopolis, a titular metropolis of Palestina Secunda, is ancient Bethsan of the Bible, as Josephus's texts prove. Its Greek name likely comes from Scythian invaders of Palestine in the seventh century before Christ, some of whom stayed behind. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a Decapolis capital through bishops and heresy.

The name first appears in Second Maccabees and the Greek Judith. Though the only Decapolis town on the Jordan's right bank, Scythopolis became civil and church metropolis of Palestina Secunda in the fourth century. Its bishops include Patrophilus, friend of Arius, present at Nicaea in 325 and at Arian councils until 360. A cruel fanatic, he ill-treated exiled Catholic bishops, above all Eusebius of Vercelli, before his deposition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebastopolis:
Sebastopolis, a titular see in Armenia Prima suffragan of Sebastia, began as Carana, a town dependent on Zela within the principality Anthony or Augustus gave to Ateporix. When the Galatian tetrarch died in 3 or 2 before Christ, Carana joined Pontus Galaticus and the Roman Empire. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a highway town to Roman culture.

Carana grew into a city from surrounding countryfolk, dating its era from its incorporation. Probably then, or a little later in 19, the name Sebastopolis appeared. Organised like other provincial cities, it worshipped the emperors and shared a district court centred on Neocaesarea. Coining from Trajan's reign, it owed its weight to the great road from Tavium in Galatia toward Sebastia and Armenia. Trajan, annexing Pontus Galaticus to a reorganised Cappadocia, made it a centre of Roman culture in a still rough land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sekanais:
The Sékanais, a Déné people living on both sides of the Rocky Mountains and properly called Tshé-kéh-ne, the People on the Rocks, are the subject of this ethnographic entry. By language they belong to the eastern Déné. The entry explains how a western band, driven across the mountains by kinsmen armed through Canadian fur traders, split off. Further splits produced the Beavers of the Peace valley and the Sarcees, later taken into the Blackfeet Confederacy.

Numbers are small, the entry reports. There were no more than 450 Sékanais proper, perhaps 550 Beavers, and 190 Sarcees. Inveterate nomads without villages or strict chiefs, they followed headmen drawn from the best-related fathers of families. The entry praises their honesty and morals. It notes polyandry, known among them alone of Déné tribes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sergiopolis:
Sergiopolis, a titular see in Augusta Euphratensis suffragan to Hierapolis, began life under its native name Rhesapha. Ptolemy, the Peutinger Table, and the Notitia Dignitatum all record it, and its name meant a paved road in Arabic. The entry identifies it with the Reseph of Kings and Isaiah, a town whose Assyrian governors are known from cuneiform records between 839 and 737 BC. It was then an important commercial center.

At Rosapha, as it was also called, the soldier Sergius was martyred under Maximian on 7 October, and the town took its official name from him. A Roman fortress stood there. Its first bishop was appointed shortly after the martyrdom, and the entry follows the see through bishops, councils, and pilgrimage fame, with the shrine of Sergius drawing visitors from across the east.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simone-de-mag:
Simone de Magistris, born in 1728 and dead on 6 October 1802, was a priest of the Roman Oratory. Pius VI made him titular Bishop of Cyrene and provost of the congregation for correcting Eastern liturgical books. He was deeply versed in Eastern languages and often received research commissions on church antiquity from Clement XIV and Pius VI. He devoted himself above all to Scripture study.

His publications include a Daniel according to the Septuagint from Origen's Tetrapla, printed at Rome in 1772 from the sole Chigi codex, with five dissertations and Hippolytus's commentary. Later came Acts of Martyrs at Ostia in 1795, the works of Dionysius of Alexandria in 1796, and acts of five Korean martyrs in 1801.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sinis:
Sinis, a titular see in Armenia Secunda suffragan to Melitene, enters the record through a correction of the Roman Curia's list. The old list carried a see of Sinita in Armenia, but the 1884 revision replaced it with Sinis, belonging to Armenia Secunda with Melitene, now Malatia, as metropolis. Ptolemy mentions a town Siniscolon in Cappadocia near Melitene by the Euphrates.

Müller identifies Siniscolon with Sinekli, a village near the Euphrates about nineteen miles north of Malatia. Yet Siniscolon seems certainly a misreading for Sinis Colonia, a form found in several manuscripts. Ramsay reads Sinis for other garbled names, placing Sinis Colonia west of Melitene, twenty-two Roman miles along the road to Caesarea. No mention of the town appears among Melitene's suffragans in Greek lists, and no bishop of it is known, so it seems never to have been a bishopric at all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ch:
The Sisters of Charity of Saint Louis began at Vannes in Brittany in 1803. Madame Molé, born de Lamoignan, founded the congregation to educate poor girls, following Bishop de Pancemont of Vannes, her director. Pius VII blessed the undertaking in 1805, but Rome's final approbation did not come until 1840.

The sisters taught poor girls living in orphanages attached to their convents, and ran pay schools to support those orphanages. The congregation lived by a spirit of penitence and mortification, under a mother-general and the bishop. It counted twenty houses in France, mostly in Brittany, but government closure of their schools drove most sisters to Canada, where they opened fourteen houses. Foundations in England followed at Minehead, Glastonbury, and Frome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-th:
Founded at Aachen in 1845 by Frances Schervier. The Sisters of the Poor of Saint Francis follow the Third Order rule of Saint Francis and care for the sick poor dependent on charity. Schervier, born 3 January 1819 to a needle manufacturer and magistrate, began by feeding and clothing the poor and visiting them at home and in hospital. In 1844 she and four companions joined the Third Order, and the next year they lived together beyond Saint James's Gate, with Frances as superior.

Cholera and smallpox in Aachen in late 1848 opened their nursing work, and an infirmary in an old Dominican building became their base. Mother Frances and twenty-three associates received the habit on 12 August 1851. Houses multiplied across Germany, reaching about 49 institutions in Europe by 1911. Six sisters sailed for Cincinnati on 24 August 1858, founding the American branch, which began building a hospital on Linn and Betts Streets, now Saint Mary's Hospital.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sitifis:
Sitifis, a titular see in Mauretania Sitifensis, stood on the road from Carthage to Cirta in Mauretania Caesarensis. Of little note under the Numidian kings, it rose when Nerva settled a colony of veterans there. When Mauretania Sitifensis was created near the end of the third century, Sitifis became its capital, and it stayed a provincial capital under the Vandals and Byzantines.

Arabs captured the town in the seventh century, and by the French occupation of 1838 it lay almost ruined. Today it is Setif, chief town of an arrondissement in Constantine, Algeria, with 15,000 inhabitants trading in cattle, cereals, leather, and cloth. Christian inscriptions survive, including one of 452 naming relics of Saint Lawrence and another naming martyrs Justus and Decurius. Augustine records a monastery, an episcopal school, and an earthquake in which 2,000 people sought baptism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-fo:
Established in 1658 to 1663, the Society of Foreign Missions of Paris was chiefly founded by Bishops Pallu and Lambert de la Motte, vicars apostolic of Tongking and Cochin China. Both crossed Persia and India on foot to reach their missions. The society evangelizes non-Christian countries by founding churches and raising native clergy under the bishops.

It is not a religious order but a congregation of secular priests. They are bound not by vows but by an approved rule, a common object, and the Paris seminary in the Rue du Bac. Members promise lifelong mission service, and the society supports them in return. By the end of the eighteenth century it counted six bishops, 135 native priests, nine seminaries, and 300,000 Christians, despite the Revolution halting its growth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-ma:
Founded at Bordeaux in 1817 by William Joseph Chaminade, the Society of Mary of Paris must not be confused with the Marists of Lyons, founded in 1816. Chaminade, born at Périgueux in 1761, ministered through the Revolution in disguise and hiding, then spent three years exiled at Saragossa. Returning to Bordeaux in 1800, he formed sodalities of men and women to repair the Revolution's damage to the Church.

Members, clerical and lay, take simple vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience, adding a fourth vow of stability in Mary's service at final profession. The Roman Curia calls them Marianists. Christian education became their chief work, and by 1908 the society counted seven provinces and one vice-province, with 53 establishments in the United States alone, including colleges, high schools, and parish schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sozopolis:
Sozopolis was a titular see on the Thracian shore of the Black Sea. It was first called Antheia, then soon renamed Apollonia for its temple of Apollo. Founded by Milesian colonists under Anaximander, it held a statue of the god thirty cubits high. Lucullus later carried that statue to Rome for the Capitol, and its coins bore Apollo's image from the fourth century before Christ into the third century after.

Later sources drop Apollonia for Sozopolis, the name found in the Periplus and the lists of bishoprics. By 1328 Cantacuzene still called it a large and populous town. Now joined to the mainland by a narrow tongue of land and known in Turkish as Sizebolou, it offers readers a small port's long passage from Greek colony to Byzantine see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aldegundis:
St. Aldegundis was a virgin and abbess of the seventh century, about 639 to 684, nearly related to the Merovingian royal house. This entry follows a daughter of Walbert and Bertilia, later honoured as saints, who lived in Hainault in Flanders. She refused marriage for virginity, left home, and received the veil from Amandus, Bishop of Maastricht.

Walking dry-shod over the Sambre, she built a small nunnery on its banks at a desert place called Malbode. That foundation grew, under the name Maubeuge, into a famous abbey of Benedictine nuns, later replaced by canonesses. Her feast falls on 30 January, and the entry notes that no contemporary life survives, though several early ones, including Hucbald's tenth-century biography, are printed by the Bollandists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-apollinari:
St. Apollinaris was one of the first great martyrs of the Church. This entry follows a bishop made by St. Peter himself for Ravenna. His miracles and preaching soon won many converts to the faith. They also drew the fury of idolaters, who beat him cruelly and drove him from the city. Found half dead on the seashore, he was kept hidden by Christians.

Captured again, he was forced to walk on burning coals and expelled a second time. Still he stayed nearby and carried on his evangelizing work. He then journeyed through the province of Aemilia. A third time he returned to Ravenna, where he was captured again. He was hacked with knives, scalded, beaten in the mouth with stones for persisting in preaching, and flung chained into a dungeon to starve.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-camillus-d:
St. Camillus de Lellis was born at Bucchianico in Abruzzo in 1550. He died at Rome on 14 July 1614. This entry follows the son of an officer with service in both the Neapolitan and French armies. His mother died in his childhood, and he grew up wholly neglected. Still a youth, he took service as a soldier with Venice, then with Naples, until his regiment disbanded in 1574.

While in service he became a confirmed gambler, and his losses at play at times left him destitute. A Franciscan friar's kindness moved him to seek admission to that order, but he was refused. He then went to Rome, where he found employment in the Hospital for Incurables. He was prompted to go there chiefly by hope of a cure for abscesses in both his feet, from which he had long suffered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-denis:
Paris honours Denis as its first bishop and martyr. This entry separates the missionary record from the famous legend of his death. Pope Fabian sent him to Gaul in the third century with fellow missionaries. He settled on the island in the Seine and built a church there. His preaching won converts, and pagan priests turned the crowd against him. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his feast to 9 October.

His companions Rusticus and Eleutherius shared his work and his execution. The early Passio supplies the details, though it is wrongly tied to Venantius Fortunatus. Best known is the image of Denis carrying his own severed head. Art has kept that image ever since. The entry lets readers see both the restorer of a battered Gallic church and the martyr legend that grew from it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-felix-of-v:
Felix of Valois, hermit of the forest of Meaux, helped found an order that bought captives free. Born in 1127, surnamed Valois for royal kin or for his native province, he gave up his possessions young and retired to dense woodland for prayer and contemplation. There John of Matha joined him with a plan: an order for redeeming captives. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Cerfroi to 4 November 1212.

After fervent prayer the pair travelled to Rome, bearing letters from the bishop of Paris. Innocent III, newly pope, received them kindly, lodged them in his palace, and weighed the project in solemn conclaves of cardinals and prelates. Convinced the men were raised up by God for the Church's good, he confirmed their order. The entry follows a hermit's solitude into an institution of mercy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-jeanne-de-:
Jeanne de Valois, queen and foundress of the Annonciades, suffered humiliation from birth and answered it with devotion. Daughter of Louis XI and Charlotte of Savoy, born in 1464, she was hated by her father for her sex and for being sickly and deformed. Sent to guardians in a lonely country château, she lost not only rank's advantages but common comforts, almost necessities. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Bourges to 4 February 1505.

Solitude and abjectness first turned her to God, giving her early a tender, practical devotion to Mary. She is said to have received a supernatural promise that she would one day found a religious family honouring Our Lady. The mysteries of Annunciation and Incarnation, as the Angelus sets them forth, shaped that devotion. Daughter of one king and wife of another, few calendar saints suffered bitterer humiliation, and few turned it to founding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-franc:
John Francis Regis, Jesuit missioner of southern France, spent his last ten years preaching village to village. Born on 31 January 1597 at Fontcouverte in Aude, he was son of Jean, a rich merchant lately ennobled for League war service, and Marguerite de Cugunhan of Languedoc's landed nobility. He was raised with Christian care. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at La Louvesc to 30 December 1640.

At fourteen he went to the Jesuit college at Béziers, exemplary in conduct, devoted, good-humoured, frank, and eager to oblige. He taught grammar at Billom, Puy-en-Velay, and Auch, studied philosophy at Tournon, and preached on feast days in nearby towns. Newly priested, he hastened to plague victims at Toulouse. From 1632 missions became his life's work, through cities and localities too many to list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-michael-de:
Michael de Sanctis, a Spanish Trinitarian of the seventeenth century, lived a life of prayer, penance, and devotion to the Eucharist. Born at Vich in Catalonia on 29 September 1591, he entered the Trinitarians at twelve. He took vows at Saragossa in 1607, then moved to the stricter Discalced branch, taking vows at Alcalá. He became a priest and was twice chosen superior at Valladolid.

He was known for long prayer, severe self-denial, and raptures during the Consecration of the Mass. He died at Valladolid on 10 April 1625, was beatified by Pius VI in 1779, and canonised by Pius IX in 1862. His feast falls on 5 July, and he is pictured kneeling before the exposed Sacrament. The entry offers a compact life of a quiet contemplative.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-tigris:
Tigris, an Irish saint and sister of Patrick, mothered five sons who all became bishops. Much obscurity clouds her life, and she is often confused with Darerca, another of Patrick's five sisters treated at length by Colgan. Her sons were Loman of Trim and Munis of Forgney, Broccaid of Emlagh and Broccen of Breaghwy, and Mugenoc of All Duimi Gluin.

Jocelyn gives her seventeen sons and five daughters instead. Tirechan and the Tripartite Life are better guides, and they name the five bishops. Her husband was named Gollit. The time and place of her death are uncertain. The entry is short, resting on Stokes's Tripartite Life and Healy's Patrick, and it suits readers tracing Patrick's remarkable family.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-vitalis:
Vitalis, a martyr of Ravenna, survives in a legend of little historical value that still built a great church. The tale says a judge named Paulinus had him racked and buried alive for encouraging the wavering Ursicinus and burying his remains. He was husband of Valeria, martyred at Milan, and father of the more famous Gervasius and Protasius.

His feast falls on 28 April, but his martyrdom's date is uncertain. The legend makes him a victim of Nero, while Baronius places him in 171 under Marcus Aurelius. Papebroch lists churches honouring him from Rome to Dalmatia, chief among them San Vitale at Ravenna, built in 541 to 546 and dedicated in 547. The entry weighs legend against the stones of Ravenna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-william-of:
William of Paris, abbot of Eskil in Denmark, restored regular observance among Danish canons. Born in 1105 to a noble French family, he became a secular canon at Ste-Geneviève-du-Mont. After Suger's reform he became a canon regular and sub-prior there when Bishop Absalom of Lund, hearing reports of his sanctity, sent Saxo Grammaticus to Paris to request his help.

William agreed, becoming abbot of Eskil, where he brought the religious back to the primitive observance of their rule. His reform steadied a diocese where discipline had decayed. He died in 1202, was canonised on 12 February 1224, and his feast is observed on 6 April. The entry is brief, resting on Saxo's mission and the reform's success.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-willigis:
Willigis, archbishop of Mainz and archchancellor of the Empire, crowned two kings and built Mainz cathedral. Of humble birth but well educated, he entered Otto I's service through Bishop Volkold of Meissen and after 971 served as chancellor of Germany. Otto II made him archbishop of Mainz and archchancellor in 975.

Benedict VII gave him the pallium in March 975, naming him Primate of Germany. On Christmas 983 he crowned Otto III at Aachen, and in June 1002 he crowned Henry II at Mainz. He presided at Frankfurt's synod in 1007, where thirty-five bishops signed John XVIII's bull erecting Bamberg diocese. Hauck calls him an ideal tenth-century bishop, demanding solid learning from his clergy. He died on 23 February 1011.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stauropolis:
Stauropolis, a titular see of Caria, began as a Lelegian city and became Aphrodisias, famed for Aphrodite. First called Megalopolis, then Ninoe, finally Aphrodisias, it stood at Mount Cadmus's foot, watered by many springs. Its celebrated temple of Aphrodite won it from Roman emperors, especially Caesar, the rights of a free city and asylum.

Apollonius, historian of Caria, was born there, as was Alexander, Aristotle's second-century commentator. Hierocles's Synecdemus and Justinian's Novel 160 still use Aphrodisias, and its bishops signed the Fifth General Council in 553. Stauropolis first appears about 640 in pseudo-Epiphanius's Ecthesis. Tauropolis, alleged as an earlier name, is a scholars' error. Le Quien lists twenty bishops of the see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sylvester-nor:
Sylvester Norris, born in Somersetshire in 1570 or 1572, was a controversial writer and English missionary priest. After minor orders at Reims in 1590, he finished his studies at the English College in Rome, was ordained, and reached the English mission in May 1596. His energy shows in his place among the appellant clergy of 1600.

After the Gunpowder Plot he was jailed in Bridewell, where he wrote to Salisbury protesting innocence and offering to labour at Rome for Catholic loyalty. Banished with forty-six priests in 1606, he joined the Jesuits, returned to England in 1611, and became superior of the Hampshire district in 1621. His Antidote of 1622 heads a long list of controversial works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synaxis:
Synaxis means gathering, assembly, or reunion, the exact Greek match for Latin collecta and a cousin of synagogue. In Christian use it names any religious assembly, whether the act of gathering or the people gathered. The verb appears often in the New Testament for religious meetings, Jewish services, and councils, and in the Apostolic Fathers for the union of the Church.

Liturgical synaxis means the Eucharist, while aliturgical synaxis means prayers, readings, and psalms alone, from which the Divine Office grew. Dionysius uses the word only for the Eucharist, and Bona finds a mystic sense of union with God in it. Benedict and Cassian carried it westward, and the Byzantine calendar still keeps it as the title of station feasts, like the Synaxis of the Seventy on 4 January.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synderesis:
Synderesis, more correctly synteresis, is the Scholastic name for habitual knowledge of the universal practical principles of moral action. Just as speculative science rests on axioms, moral conduct rests on first principles. Science holds that a thing cannot both be and not be, and that the whole is greater than its part. Morals hold that good must be done, evil avoided, and parents honoured.

Any sane person who grasps these truths admits them at once. The Scholastics credit that readiness to a natural habit stamped on the mind, which they call synderesis. Conscience differs from it: conscience judges a particular act right or wrong, while synderesis holds the general principles themselves. Thomas Aquinas states the doctrine in his Summa, First Part, question 79.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tanis:
Tanis, in Egyptian Zani and Hebrew Zoan, was a titular see suffragan of Pelusium. It was capital of Lower Egypt's fourteenth district. It stood on a Nile branch that took its name. It counts among the world's oldest cities, attested under Pepi I of the sixth dynasty. It flourished under the twelfth dynasty and the Hyksos shepherd kings. The nineteenth, twenty-first, and twenty-third dynasties made it their capital.

Under the shepherd kings, Jews settled nearby in Goshen. At Tanis, home of Rameses II, Moses and Aaron worked wonders. Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Jeremiah all denounced the city. Jeremiah followed fleeing Jews there after Nebuchadnezzar's conquest. Its earliest bishop was the Melitian Eudaemon early in the fourth century. Hermion followed in 362, and Apollonius appeared at Ephesus and in 458.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tentyris:
Tentyris, or Tentyra, was a titular suffragan see of Ptolemais in Thebaid Secunda. The city was capital of its nome. Amelineau gives its real name as Nikentori or Nitentori, meaning willow wood or willow earth. Others derive it from Hathor, or Aphrodite, specially worshipped there. The crocodile counted as the city's deity, and was venerated in other Egyptian cities too, causing many quarrels, notably with Ombos.

Little is known of Christianity there, with only two ancient bishops named. Pachymius was a companion of Melece early in the fourth century, and Serapion, or Aprion, was a friend of the monk Pachomius, whose celebrated convent of Tabennisi lay in his diocese. Today the town is Denderah, with 6,000 people in the district of Qeneh. The temple of Hathor still stands, built on a more ancient foundation from Cheops' reign, where the celebrated zodiac now in Paris was found.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-terenuthis: Terenuthis was a titular see, suffragan of Antinoë in Thebais Prima. Le Quien names two bishops: Arsinthius in 404 and Eulogius at Ephesus in 431. Monks sometimes sheltered there during raids by the barbarian Maziks, and John Moschus visited early in the seventh century. The town appears often in Christian Coptic literature. Today Tarraneh in Beherah province replaces it, its ruins lying about a mile and a quarter west, with 1,330 people. About nine and a quarter miles away stand the Lakes of Nitria and Scetis, with their famous lauras.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodosiopoli:
Thracian see Theodosiopolis, first called Apros, is the old city traced in this short entry. At first Apros or Aproi, later Colonia Claudia Aprensis in Ptolemy's Geography, it ranked in the fourth century, in Ammianus's words, as chief city south of Heraclea. Theodosius I or II gave it the grand name Theodosiopolis, rarely used, while plain Apros stayed on people's lips.

Heraclea's suffragan at first, Apros rose by 640 to a self-ruled archbishopric, a rank it still held in 1170. Romanus signed as Metropolitan of Apros in 1179, and Manuel I Comnenus's lists of that age agree. The see faded at the end of the fourteenth century or the start of the fifteenth, leaving a name that outlived its town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thibaris:
Byzacene see Thibaris, fixed by an inscription at Henshir Hamamet, is the small town described here. Rome's official list puts it in Byzacena, though in truth it lay in Africa Proconsularis. Ruins stand in a plain watered by the Wady Tibar, which kept the town's name, about five miles northeast of Djebba near Djebel Gorra Tunaiai. Galena and calamine mines at Djebba worked since ancient times.

Cyprian's letter to Thibaris's faithful, Epistle 66, mentions the mines. Chief ruins are an aqueduct and a Christian church, and nearby stands Saint Joseph of Tibar's orphanage, where White Fathers took in mainly Algerian Kabyles. Two bishops are known: Vincent at Carthage in 256 and Victor at Carthage in 411, facing Donatist rival Victorian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thmuis:
Thmuis was an ancient city in Lower Egypt, on a canal east of the Nile between its Tanitic and Mendesian branches. Once capital of its own district, it kept its own administration in the fourth century and stood apart from the prefect of Alexandria. The entry follows the city through the Arab conquest, after which it faded and vanished following the Turkish conquest.

Its ruins lie at Tell el-Mei, a few miles from Senbelaouin on the railway between Zagazig and Mansurah. Nine bishops are named, from the martyrs Phileas and Donatus through Liberius at Nicaea in 325, Serapion, Ptolemaeus at Seleucia, and Aristobulus at Ephesus. The last three were Monophysites of the Middle Ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-a-kemp:
Thomas a Kempis, born at Kempen around 1379, is best known as the author of the Imitation of Christ, one of the most widely read works of Christian devotion. The son of artisan parents, he left home at thirteen for the schools at Deventer, then joined the Canons Regular at Mount St. Agnes near Zwolle. He was clothed as a novice in 1406 and ordained priest in 1413.

Much of the entry weighs the long dispute over who wrote the Imitation, setting out the case for Thomas against rival claims. It also follows his quiet monastic career, his chronicle of Mount St. Agnes, and his other writings. He died in 1471, after a life spent in study, copying books and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-tallis:
Thomas Tallis, an English composer born about 1514, kept his place at court through four reigns while holding fast to the old faith. A chorister at St. Paul's Cathedral, he became organist of Waltham Abbey in 1536 and lost the post at the dissolution in 1540. In 1542 he joined the Chapel Royal, where he served Henry VIII, Edward VI, Mary and Elizabeth in turn.

Elizabeth herself allowed the avowed Catholic to stay, and with William Byrd he held the valuable monopoly of printing music and ruled music paper from 1575 until his death. His output was huge, from masses such as Salve Intemerata to a forty-part motet, a feat of polyphony. Most of his music went unprinted in his lifetime, but modern editors have brought it back into use. He died in November 1585.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tiberiopolis:
Tiberiopolis was a titular see in Phrygia Pacatiana, named by Ptolemy, Socrates and Hierocles. It struck its own coins at least from Trajan's reign, though its exact site is unknown, somewhere near Egri Gueuz in the region of Kutahya. Greek lists of bishoprics count it among the suffragans of Laodicea. In the eighth century it passed to the metropolitan see of Hierapolis, where it stayed until the thirteenth century.

Five of its bishops are known, all from their presence at councils. They are Eustathius at Constantinople in 536, Silas there in 553, Anastasius in 692, Michael at Nicaea in 787 and Theoctistus at Constantinople in 879. Council lists and coinage thus fix the see's place in the church geography of Asia Minor, even though its exact site remains unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tingis:
Tingis, now Tangier, is an ancient Phoenician town at the strait between Africa and Spain. Greek legend credits its founding to the giant Antaeus, or to Sophax, son of Hercules. Under Rome it became first a free city, then a colony under Augustus, and capital of Mauretania Tingitana. Portuguese, Spanish and English rulers followed, and England gave it up in 1684.

By the nineteenth century it belonged to Morocco and held about 40,000 people, half Muslim, with 10,000 Jews and 9,000 Europeans. Late in the third century it saw the martyrdoms of Marcellus and Cassian. Under Portugal it became a suffragan of Lisbon, and in 1570 it was joined to Ceuta. It is now home to the prefect apostolic of Morocco, served by the Friars Minor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-titiopolis:
Titiopolis was a titular see subject to Seleucia Trachaea in Isauria, one of the cities of the Isaurian Decapolis. Le Quien names three bishops: Artemius at Constantinople in 381, Mompraeus at Chalcedon in 451, and Domitus at the Trullan Council in 692. The see appears in the sixth-century list of Antioch, and its exact site is unknown.

About 732 the province of Isauria passed to the Patriarchate of Constantinople. Titiopolis appears in that church's lists thereafter, including those of Leo the Wise about 900 and Constantine Porphyrogenitus about 940. Hierocles, George of Cyprus and Constantine Porphyrogenitus all count it among Isaurian cities. Its history thus survives in council records and geography lists rather than in ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-titular-archd:
Hierapolis, or Mabog, was a titular archdiocese and metropolis of the Euphrates province in the Patriarchate of Antioch. Its name, meaning Holy City, recalls the famed temple of the Syrian goddess Atargatis, also called Derceto, where the dove was sacred and the goddess took the form of a woman-fish. Pilgrims came twice a year to pour water through an opening in the temple floor.
