Crassus plundered the temple on his Parthian campaign, and under Seleucids and Romans the city grew into a great caravan halt between Seleucia and Babylon. As a military stronghold it gathered Roman and Byzantine armies against Persia. Julian the Apostate stopped there before marching on Sapor, Chosroes spared it in 540 for a heavy fine, and Justinian rebuilt its walls, whose towers still stand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trajanopolis:
Trajanopolis was a titular metropolitan see of Rhodope, owing its founding or restoration to Trajan. Le Quien lists many bishops. They include Theodulus, persecuted by Arians in the fourth century, and Syncletius, friend of Chrysostom. Later come Peter at Ephesus in 431, Basilius at Chalcedon in 451, Abundantius in 521 and Eleusius in 553, then Cudumenes about 1270 and Germanus in 1352.

About 640 the see held two suffragans, and by the early tenth century seven. St. Glyceria, a second-century martyr honoured on 13 May, was born there. Villehardouin names the town, Joannitza of Bulgaria captured and pillaged it in 1206, and by 1564 its metropolitan title had passed to neighbouring Maronia, proof the city itself was destroyed. Viquesnel and Dumont found its site on the Maritza near Ouroundjik.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trapezopolis:
A titular see in Phrygia Pacatiana, suffragan to Laodicea, whose early history is unknown. Ptolemy and Pliny place the town in Caria, while Socrates, Hierocles and the episcopal lists put it in Phrygia Pacatiana, where it stayed among Laodicea's suffragans until the thirteenth century.

Its coins show close trade with Attouda, now Assar, and its site is sought nearby, most likely at Kadi Keui in the district of Denizli. Le Quien names six of its bishops, from Hierophilius before 400 through Asclepiades at Ephesus in 431 and John at Chalcedon in 451 to Leo at Constantinople in 879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tunis:
A French protectorate on the northern coast of Africa, settled by Phoenicians about the twelfth century before Christ. Their colonies, including Utica, Carthage and Hadrumetum, fell under Carthage's sway, and after Carthage fell in 146 B.C. Rome made the country the Province of Africa, one of Italy's granaries.

Vandals took it in 439, Belisarius retook it for the Eastern Empire in 533, and Arabs overran it from 648, founding Kairouan in 670 and reducing Carthage to ruins in 697. Charles V captured Tunis in July 1535 and freed nearly 20,000 Christian slaves, but the Turks established supremacy in 1574 after Don Juan's brief recapture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Three schools made Paris famous early: the palace school, the school of Notre-Dame, and that of Sainte-Geneviève. Royal decline dragged the first down with it, while the other two, very old like other cathedral and abbey schools, remain faintly outlined in their early centuries. The palace school's glory long eclipsed theirs, until in time it gave way to them entirely. Both centres drew many students, and their masters won esteem for learning.

Only in the tenth century does a renowned professor appear at Sainte-Geneviève: Hubold, who came from Liège to continue his studies. The entry follows the schools' growth into the university, its nations, faculties, and colleges, and its commanding place in medieval thought. It covers the great masters, the quarrels with crown and pope, and the university's long dominance of European learning.

St Louis University, probably the oldest university west of the Mississippi, was founded in the city of St Louis in 1818 by Bishop Louis William Du Bourg of Louisiana. Since 1827 it has stood under the Society of Jesus. On 16 November 1818 Du Bourg opened St Louis Academy, placing it under Father François Niel and other secular clergy of the cathedral. In 1820 the name changed to St Louis College.

The college thrived, but the secular clergy, burdened with parish duties, struggled to staff its chairs. Du Bourg, once president of Georgetown College, soon planned to hand the college to the Jesuits, who took charge in 1827. The entry follows the school's growth, its charter, its faculties, and its place in the Catholic life of the American West, from a frontier academy to a university.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-uranopolis:
Uranopolis was a titular see of Asia Minor, suffragan of Ancyra in Galatia Prima, yet it is sought in vain in any list of bishoprics or geography, ancient or modern. The entry explains the puzzle: the name is a faulty spelling or variant of Verinopolis, named in honour of Verina, mother-in-law of Emperor Zeno. Le Quien names three bishops of the see.

They are Stephen, present at the Trullan Council in 692, Anthimus at the second Council of Nicaea in 787, and Sisinnius at the Constantinople councils of 869 and 878. The diocese appears about 640 in the Ecthesis of pseudo-Epiphanius, about 900 in Leo the Philosopher's list under the name Stauros, and about 940 in Constantine Porphyrogenitus's list. A short entry that solves a name's mystery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ut-queant-lax:
Ut queant laxis resonare fibris is the first line of a hymn honouring St John the Baptist. The Roman Breviary splits it into three parts for the feast of John's Nativity on 24 June. Ut queant laxis serves Vespers, Antra deserti teneris sub annis serves Matins, and O nimis felix, meritique celsi serves Lauds. With most hymnologists, Dreves credits Paul the Deacon with the hymn.

The hymn runs in Sapphic stanzas, and its first stanza holds a famous place in music history. The notes matching the opening syllables of its six half-lines give the first six notes of the C scale. That fact gave us the syllable names Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La for notes. The entry traces the hymn's text, authorship, and musical fame in compact form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-thul:
John Thulis was an English martyr born at Up Holland in Lancashire, probably about 1568, who suffered at Lancaster on 18 March 1615 or 1616. He reached the English College at Reims on 25 May 1583 and Cardinal Guise gave him tonsure on 23 September following. He left for Rome on 27 March 1590, was ordained priest there, and was sent out on the mission in April 1592.

He seems to have been held prisoner at Wisbech in Cambridgeshire when he signed the letter of 8 November 1598 favouring the archpriest's institution. He signed the letter of 17 November 1600 against it. Later he laboured in Lancashire, where William, fifteenth Earl of Derby, arrested him and committed him to Lancaster Castle, where his fellow martyr Roger Wrenno, a weaver, was confined. The two escaped one evening before the Lent assizes but were recaptured the next day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-victor-vitens:
Victor Vitensis was an African bishop of Vita in Byzacena, born probably about 430, whose importance rests on his History of the African Persecution under the Vandal kings Geiseric and Huneric. Formerly in five books, now usually three, its first book, on Geiseric's reign from 427 to 477, draws on others' accounts. The second and third, on Huneric, form a strictly contemporary narrative of events the author largely witnessed.

No exception can be taken to Victor's accuracy except that he always exaggerates, though allowance for the feeling under which he wrote shows he records little that did not happen. His history illuminates social and religious life in Carthage and the African liturgy of the period. Preserves valuable documents found nowhere else, including the orthodox confession Eugenius of Carthage drew up for presentation to Huneric at the 484 conference of Catholic and Arian bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincent-of-be:
Vincent of Beauvais was a thirteenth-century Dominican priest and encyclopedist whose personal history is little known, his birth and death commonly given as 1190 and 1264. Thought to have joined the Dominicans at Paris shortly after 1218, he spent almost all his religious life at Beauvais monastery, apart from visits to his royal patron Louis IX at Royaumont.

With Louis's help in buying books, this industrious man undertook a systematic, comprehensive treatment of all branches of human knowledge, the Great Mirror. Its first part, Mirror of Nature, runs to thirty-two books and 3,718 chapters on theology, psychology, physiology, cosmography, physics, botany, zoology, mineralogy. Agriculture, including an early reference to using the magnet for navigation. Its second part, Mirror of Doctrine, in seventeen books and 2,374 chapters, treats logic, rhetoric, poetry, geometry, astronomy, instincts, and passions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilgefortis:
Wilgefortis is a fabulous female saint, also called Uncumber, Kummernis, Comera, Liberata, and many other names. Legend makes her a Christian daughter of a pagan King of Portugal who, to keep her vow of chastity and evade her father's command to marry a pagan prince. Prayed God to disfigure her body, whereupon God caused a beard to grow on her chin and her father had her crucified.

Joined to the legend is the tale of a destitute fiddler who, playing before her image, received one of her golden boots. Was condemned to death for stealing it, and, granted his request to play before her again, saw her kick off her other boot before all, proving his innocence. A robed, crowned, long-haired crucified Saviour, popularly believed Nicodemus's work, since the eleventh century no longer the usual way of picturing Christ on the cross.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-na:
William of Nangis was a thirteenth-century Benedictine chronicler at Saint-Denis near Paris. All that is known of him is his monkhood there; scholars split on whether he died before 22 July 1300 or after 1303. His chronicle runs from creation to 1300, but before 1133 it leans wholly on Sigebert of Gembloux and carries little fresh weight, and even later it ranks as secondary. After his death unknown Saint-Denis monks carried it to 1340, and John of Venette to 1368.

William also made a short summary, the Chronicon Abbreviatum Regum Francorum for 845 to 1300. Delisle lately found its original in the Vatican; it had been known only in the author's own French version. He further wrote lives of Louis VIII, Louis IX, and Philip III the Bold. Research by Brosien shows the latter two lives trace to the monk Primatus, padded with long extracts from Geoffrey of Beaulieu and Gilo of Reims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zenonopolis:
Zenonopolis is the Asia Minor titular see, suffragan of Seleucia Trachaea in Isauria, shortened in the Roman Curia to Zenopolis. It was Emperor Zeno's native village, formerly known as Codissos. In Antioch's sixth-century Notitia Episcopatuum it ranks among Seleucia's suffragans. About 732 Isauria joined Constantinople's patriarchate, and Zenopolis appears about 940 in Constantine Porphyrogenitus's Notitia, though placed in Pamphylia. George of Cyprus mentions the city in the seventh century, and Constantine Porphyrogenitus lists it as a city of the Decapolis.

Le Quien names two bishops: Eulalius, present at Constantinople's council in 681, and Marcus, at Nicaea in 787. Gennadius, who attended the fifth council in 553 as bishop of Zenonopolis in Pamphylia, was very probably a prelate of this see. Zenonopolis is today Isnebol in the caza of Ermenek and the vilayet of Adana. It must not be confused with another Zenonopolis in Lycia.
catullus-poems-ellis:
Catullus, a Roman poet of the first century BCE, wrote short poems of love, friendship, and attack. Robinson Ellis translated the complete poems and fragments into English. His Lesbia poems remain the most famous part of the set.

Catullus swings between tender devotion and furious insult, sometimes within a page. He pioneered a personal, polished lyric style drawn from Greek models. Poems to his dead brother and to Lesbia's pet sparrow show his range. Some pieces are frankly obscene, and Victorian readers often skipped them. Ellis's notes help students through the dense allusions. Latin poetry rarely feels this immediate or this alive.
cousin-phillis:
Elizabeth Gaskell's Cousin Phillis opens with a lad's pride in his first lodgings. Paul Manning, seventeen, sits in a three-cornered room over a pastry-cook's shop in Eltham. His father, a mechanic with inventive genius, has got him a clerk's place under the engineer building the branch line to Hornby. On Sundays Paul walks to Hope Farm, where his cousin Phillis Holman lives. Phillis is better read than the narrator: Latin, Greek, and Dante are her evening company.

Then Mr. Holdsworth, the engineer, falls ill at the farm and is nursed by Phillis into a love neither declares. He leaves for Canada, and a brain fever does the rest. Readers get Gaskell's most perfect short work here, an idyll where one unspoken sentence carries all the tragedy.

govdocs-archive_org-LaroucheEIRTheSunNev:
The Sun Never Sets on the New British Empire is a special offprint of Executive Intelligence Review, the magazine of Lyndon LaRouche's movement, issued in June 1996. EIR publishes the movement's analysis of world affairs. Its theme here is announced in the title: British imperial power, in new forms, still rules.

The text lays out the LaRouche movement's case that finance, intelligence, and old imperial networks direct modern events from London. Friend and foe alike class EIR's worldview as its own; the offprint states it at length and in house style. The piece is held as political journalism from the movement's press, in full, for students of that current in American politics.
govdocs-archive_org-SinnettAlfredPercyTh:
Alfred Percy Sinnett, the theosophist who wrote Esoteric Buddhism and The Occult World, published The Rationale of Mesmerism in 1892 with Houghton, Mifflin. Mesmerism, the practice of inducing trances through an unseen influence, was then caught between stage entertainment and serious science.

Sinnett sets out to explain how mesmerism might actually work, arguing that its effects are real and can be reasoned about rather than dismissed as fraud. He draws on reported cases and on the occult theory he was known for. The book shows a leading Victorian occultist trying to give his subject a rational footing.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAJohnstoneIsa:
Kenneth Bredemeier reported for the Washington Post from Miami on October 24, 1978, on a custody fight with an unusual shape. A Miami court had delayed the return to District of Columbia police of Jorge A. Zimeri-Safie, a Guatemalan businessman and gun inventor.

At the center sat an odd offer: a Washington homicide detective proposed to take personal custody of Zimeri-Safie himself. Cases crossing borders, agencies, and courts produce such tangles, and newspaper court reporting is often the only public record of them. The article preserves the proceedings as they stood that October, in the Post's account.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CivicGroups_Civ:
The Associated Press reported on August 13 on a new entry in Miami's crowded exile politics: an organization called Civic Group. Its leader was Jose Perez San Roman, who had commanded the exile brigade in the Bay of Pigs invasion.

San Roman's name carried the invasion's authority and its grievances, and new exile groups formed around such men for years after 1961, each promising a road back to Havana. A wire story of a few paragraphs is often the only trace such a group left in print. The article is preserved as the record of Civic Group's public debut.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DominicanCrisis:
When crisis broke out in the Dominican Republic, the U.S. Department of State issued a publication called The Dominican Crisis: The Hemisphere Acts. It compiles the official statements of President Lyndon B. Johnson, Secretary of State Dean Rusk, and diplomat Ellsworth Bunker. Together they present the administration's public case for its actions.

A compilation like this one is the government explaining itself in its own chosen words. Readers can follow how each official framed the intervention and what reasons were offered at the time. It remains a basic source for anyone studying how Washington justified its moves in the Caribbean.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FlammondeParis_:
Harold Weisberg wrote to Paris Flammonde on October 5, 1970 with an accusation, not a greeting. Weisberg charged that Flammonde had plagiarized his work extensively in a book on the Garrison case. The letter presses the charge directly on the man he believed had taken his research.

Both men wrote about Jim Garrison's investigation, a small field where priority meant reputation. Weisberg guarded his findings fiercely and said so in writing. The letter preserves the dispute in his own words, a record of how bitter authorship fights inside assassination research could become.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GarrisonJimCrim: A news article covers the 1973 criminal trial of Jim Garrison, the New Orleans district attorney who had prosecuted men for the Kennedy assassination. The article describes his supporters gathered in the corridor outside the courtroom. Its text is garbled, and neither the publication nor the author can be identified, so the piece survives as an unnamed news report on the prosecutor in the dock.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HollisJeanLolli: Jean Lollis Hollis wrote on October 20, 1984 to Gary Mack at KXAS-TV, the Dallas television station. Mack covered the Kennedy assassination for the station and heard from viewers with memories and claims for decades. The surviving record gives the writer, the recipient, and the date but no contents, so the letter stands as dated viewer correspondence to a Dallas newsroom.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JonesHarris_Jon:
An FBI memorandum from A. Rosen to Mr. Belmont, dated March 6, 1964, concerns Jones Harris of New York City. Rosen recommends that a letter be sent to the President's Commission to clarify information about Harris. The recommendation answers the commission's own letter of February 24, 1964 asking about the man.

The Warren Commission and the Bureau corrected and clarified their way through hundreds of names. A memo proposing a clarifying letter is that machinery at its most ordinary and most revealing. The record shows how a citizen's name moved between the two bodies until its file made sense.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PosnerGeraldBoo:
An unidentified author wrote this extended critique of Gerald Posner's 'Case Closed.' Posner's 1993 book argued that Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone, and it was praised widely. The critique attacks that acclaim, above all in U.S. News & World Report. It also attacks the book's promotion on television.

The fight over 'Case Closed' was a fight over who owned the story thirty years on. A bestselling vindication of the Warren Commission drew the research community's full fire. This writer aims at the reception as much as the text: the reviews, the covers, the broadcasts. The critique preserves that backlash in detail, an argument that the verdict was sold before it was read.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SharrettChristo:
Christopher B. Sharrett of Doylestown, Pennsylvania, wrote this letter to Harold Weisberg on April 8, 1977. Sharrett resents what he calls Weisberg's 'condescending, vitriolic tone.' He defends the staff of the House Select Committee on Assassinations. They were working, he writes, under intense pressure, with insufficient funding and no access to documents.

Weisberg attacked the committee as he had attacked the Warren Commission, and some readers answered back. Sharrett's letter is the defense's turn: an outsider asking the critic to credit the staff's conditions. It preserves a genuine argument inside the research world of 1977, between a man who trusted no official inquiry and a reader who thought this one deserved its chance.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_197:
On November 4, 1979, Iranian students seized the American embassy in Tehran and began a hostage crisis lasting 444 days. Malcolm Byrne edited this briefing book, number 689, published forty years later. The takeover carried long-standing consequences for Iran, the United States, and global politics.

Documents show national security adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski proposing that Washington consider replacing Ayatollah Khomeini. He even raised direct intervention. President Jimmy Carter declined those paths. The record thus shows both the pressure for drastic action and a president refusing it, inside a crisis that helped end his presidency and froze two countries into enmity.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
During the Cuban Missile Crisis, President Kennedy's first task after deciding on a blockade was telling America's allies. This briefing book covers those NATO briefings, sixty years on. The British ambassador was the first outsider to learn of the blockade decision.

British officials were also told of an American preemptive nuclear strike plan, to be used if the Soviets moved against West Berlin. Belgium's foreign minister said he preferred that allies get twenty-four hours' notice of such plans. The documents show alliance management at the edge of nuclear war: partners informed late, asked to trust decisions that could end their own countries.
jim-davis:
Jim Davis is a boys' adventure novel by John Masefield, published in 1911. Jim tells his own story, starting with his birth in 1800 at Newnham-on-Severn in Gloucestershire. His mother died on the day of the battle of Trafalgar in 1805, and his father four years later. An uncle from Devonshire then took the orphaned boy away from his old home.

The opening chapter lingers on small, sharp memories: masons building a great house, and gypsies camping by the river. It recalls apples from a captain who had killed a man in Spain. Jim's first coach ride scares and thrills him in equal measure. Bacon and eggs at a Bristol inn count as a great treat. These early scenes set up a boyhood that soon turns toward the sea and smuggling.
life-its-true-genesis:
R. W. Wright wrote this 1884 second edition on the origin of life. Catalog metadata credits Horatius Flaccus, but the title page names Wright. His preface opens with Isaiah's call to those who thirst for knowledge. Biblical texts in Hebrew and Greek head the opening pages.

Chapters study seeds, their distribution, vitality, and migration between regions. Wright asks what life is and reviews competing theories. He refutes materialistic theories and judges Darwinism from a vitalist standpoint. The book argues for a spiritual principle behind living things. Forest growth alternations and interglacial periods occupy middle chapters. Isaiah's rain and snow text anchors his law of life.
life-of-john-coleridge-patteson-missiona:
An 1873 edition presents Yonge's life of Bishop Patteson. John Coleridge Patteson led the Melanesian mission until 1871. Contents run from his childhood at home, 1827 to 1838. Eton boyhood and Balliol undergraduate years follow in order.

His curacy at Alfington precedes the voyage out in 1855. Chapters track St. John's College, LifU, Mota, and Kohimarama. His episcopate and the Norfolk Island college fill later chapters. The last eighteen months, 1870 to 1871, close the life. St. Barnabas College on Norfolk Island occupies chapter eleven. His fellowship at Merton preceded the Alfington curacy years. Norfolk Island later housed the mission college named for Saint Barnabas.
luther-examined-and-reexamined-a-review-:
Luther Examined and Reexamined reviews Catholic attacks on the Reformer. W. H. T. Dau, a professor at Concordia Seminary in St. Louis, wrote it. Concordia Publishing House issued the book in 1917. Its subtitle adds a plea for revaluation of Luther.

Dau opens with pity for writers tasked with fighting Luther forever. He quotes a Catholic author calling today's problem 'still the Luther problem.' Rome, he argues, cannot admit her moral defeat in the Reformation. Chapter by chapter he answers charges against Luther's life and teaching. The book is a firm Lutheran defense, written for the four-hundredth anniversary year. It shows the old quarrel still alive in 1917.
lysis:
Lysis is a short dialogue by Plato, in Benjamin Jowett's translation. Jowett's introduction notes that it never answers its own question. That question is simple to ask: what is friendship? Socrates puts it to two Athenian boys, Lysis and Menexenus.

The talk unfolds in a wrestling school, amid Greek daily life. Socrates asks whether friends must be alike or unlike. He tests whether friendship springs from need, from goodness, or from desire. Each answer fails, yet the search itself delights. Lysis is a noble, beautiful youth, and Socrates treats him gently. The dialogue is philosophy's first charming look at friendship. It ends in happy puzzlement, as Plato often does.
maha-bharata-the-epic-of-ancient-india-c:
The Maha-bharata, condensed into English verse by Romesh C. Dutt, appeared in 1899. J. M. Dent published it at London in that year. Dutt dedicated his work to the Marquis of Ripon. He thanked Ripon for just rule and self-government in India.

His twelve books follow the great epic's famous arc. A tournament and a bride's choice open the tale. The fatal dice game drives the princes into exile. Then come the falls of Bhishma, Drona, and Karna in battle. Funeral rites and the horse sacrifice close the story. Dutt made India's national epic readable in one volume. His verse is plain, swift, and dignified.
mary-at-the-farm-and-book-of-recipes-com:
Edith M. Thomas published Mary at the Farm in 1915. Mary visits among the Pennsylvania Germans, and notes what she learns. A house poem at the front sets the book's warm tone.

The poem praises work done with a glad heart from dawn to night. It speaks of making pay stretch, with a bit left for a rainy day. Sewing, mending, cooking, and sweeping fill the farm wife's full and skilled day. Recipes gathered on the visit form the book's second half. Farm meals and German home ways stand side by side in it.
massacre-at-paris:
Christopher Marlowe wrote The Massacre at Paris, a stage play in short scenes. The cast list names the King of France and Catherine, his mother. Navarre, Condy, and the Lord High Admiral stand near them.

The Duke of Guise enters early and drives much of the plot. Scenes move from court talk to soldiers sent out to kill. The Admiral's body is borne in, and men kneel with books in prayer. Marlowe packs royal plots and street bloodshed into swift, stark scenes. Ramus in his study and kneeling church folk show the stakes. The play stays with the court that set the killing in train.
nasa-tm-19630002676-static-stability-and:
Cornelius Driver and M. Leroy Spearman wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-47, in September 1959. It tests a scale airplane model with an odd tail layout. The tail surfaces sit outboard of the wing tips, past the wings. Tests ran at Mach 2.01, just over twice the speed of sound.

The study measures static stability and control for that layout. In plain terms, it asks if the model wants to fly straight. It also asks if its controls can hold a steady path. Odd tail spots were being tried for fast jets then. Wind data like this told designers which layouts were safe to build.
nasa-tm-19630004032-static-stability-and:
George M. Ware wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-451, on a lens-shaped craft. The shape is called lenticular, like a lentil or a flying saucer. The craft was meant for manned reentry and a glide landing. Ware tested its stability at slow, subsonic speeds.

His summary says the craft could make a high-drag reentry. After slowing, it would glide down to a landing like a plane. Slow flight is where odd shapes can wobble or stall. Ware measured static stability and pitch control in that range. The work tested whether a saucer shape could be both a safe capsule and a flyable glider.
nasa-tm-19650003196-investigation-of-aer:
Paul G Fournier and William C Sleeman Jr, at Langley Research Center, studied two supersonic-cruise aircraft shapes at high subsonic speed. Both shapes placed their tail surfaces outboard of the wing tips, an unusual layout. The work dates from 1960, in NASA Memorandum X-293.

Even a fast cruise aircraft must fly slowly near the ground. So the pair examined stability and control at the slower end of flight. Their tunnel work shows how these outboard-tail shapes behave there. That balance between fast cruise and safe slow flight was a central design problem.
nasa-tm-19660007941-the-motion-of-trappe:
Gilbert D Mead at Goddard presented this paper in Bergen, Norway, in August 1965, on particles trapped in Earth's magnetic field. Solar wind distorts that field, squeezing it on the Sun side and stretching it behind Earth. Charged particles caught in the field bounce and drift within it. Mead studies their motion in the distorted shape, not in a simple model field.

Trapped particles form the radiation belts that spacecraft must cross. Their motion decides where dose is worst and where it is mild. A distorted-field treatment gives more honest paths than a neat dipole picture. The paper was given at an institute devoted to trapped radiation studies.
nasa-tm-19660024027-static-stability-and:
Charles F Whitcomb and Willard E Foss Jr tested two pyramid-shaped reentry models in Langley's nine by twelve inch blowdown tunnel at Mach 3.05. Each model is a right triangular pyramid with a large dihedral angle. Base-mounted controls could be deflected during the runs. The aim was the static stability of a blunt, lifting shape of a kind then being widely studied.

Longitudinal stability proved generally satisfactory for both models, the summary reports. One model's results also agreed well with a similar model tested at low speeds. Agreement across speed ranges builds trust in a new shape. Pyramid bodies were candidate entry vehicles, and tunnel proof of their stability came before any thought of flight.
nasa-tm-19680001039-measurement-and-inte:
J. P. Meyer, Donald E. Hagge, and Frank B. McDonald, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in August 1967. It measures the isotopic makeup of hydrogen and helium nuclei arriving as cosmic rays, at energies below seventy-five million electron volts per nucleon. Sorting isotopes helps scientists work out where cosmic rays are born and what happens to them in transit.

Detectors on the OGO I and IMP III satellites measured the isotope energy spectra during 1965 and 1966. The deuterium share of the flux rose steeply with energy, while the helium-3 share sat near five percent and fell at lower energies. Results agreed qualitatively with a University of Chicago group's measurements. To interpret the patterns, the authors modeled deuterium and helium-3 created when heavier nuclei fragment in interstellar space. A Monte Carlo calculation then followed protons and helium nuclei from their source to Earth.
nasa-tm-19720022853-quantitative-x-ray-d:
Ralph G Garlick of the Lewis Research Center developed these analysis methods in September 1972, as NASA TM X-2627. Superalloy parts grow oxide scales as they oxidize in hot service. Knowing exactly which oxides are present, and how much, guides alloy design. X-ray diffraction can identify those oxides from their crystal patterns. Garlick's methods turned that identification into firm numbers. Five oxides common on superalloys were covered by the work.

The methods held their error near a tenth of the amount reported. That accuracy assumed well studied samples matched to made standards. Garlick demonstrated one technique on flakes from oxidation tests. The test alloy was the cobalt based superalloy WI-52. Its spalled scales showed what the method could measure in practice. Turbine and furnace alloy work both used such checks.
new-atlantis:
Francis Bacon wrote New Atlantis near the end of his life, and his executor Dr Rowley published it in 1627. That was the year after Bacon died. An opening note in this copy dates the writing to about 1623, after Bacon's fall from power.

The tale pictures Bensalem, an ideal island state built on faith and public spirit. Its great college, Solomon's House, stands for planned study of nature. The note says Bacon there foresaw much of modern research, in pure science and in applied work alike. No other short piece by Bacon, the note claims, shows his hopes for knowledge and for his country so well.
official-report-of-the-exploration-of-th:
Newton Chittenden wrote this official report for British Columbia. He sent it to the government in November 1884. The Queen Charlotte Islands lie off the Pacific coast. The report says they number over 150 islands and islets. Their full length reaches about 156 miles.

Chittenden describes coasts, positions, and the main large islands. Graham, Moresby, and other islands make up most land area. The report records firsthand survey work for officials. It now serves as a close record of the islands then. He submitted the report as the servant of the province. Dixon Entrance parts Graham Isle from the Alaska isle group. His note home is dated at Victoria in late fall.
patty-in-paris: Hosted here, the sample shows only the front matter of Patty in Paris, the title page, contents, and list of illustrations, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Carolyn Wells and dates the book to September 1907 in New York. The contents follow Patty from plans and good-byes through days at sea to sightseeing in Paris, excursions to Versailles, Chantilly, and St. Germain, shopping, and a New Year fete.
pee-wee-harris: The sample hosted here shows only the front matter of Pee-wee Harris, the title page, dedication, and the start of the contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Percy Keese Fitzhugh, author of the Tom Slade and Roy Blakeley books, and H. S. Barbour as illustrator. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York in 1922 with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. The first contents entries are "The Battle of the Banana" and "Enter Pepsy."
phyllis: The sample hosted for this entry shows only the front matter of Phyllis, the title page and list of illustrations, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Maria Thompson Daviess, author of The Tinder Box and The Melting of Molly, with illustrations by Percy D. Johnson. The Century Company published the novel in New York in 1914, and the frontispiece caption reads: down that garden path I flew.
podcast-joerogan-WGc4CsTVxis:
The psychology of cult members and fanatics drives a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Rogan takes up the question his show keeps meeting from the outside: what makes a person hand their mind to a group, a leader, or a cause?

The talk moves through famous cult cases and the traits their followers shared, from loneliness to the hunger for certainty. Rogan asks where fandom ends and fanaticism begins, a line his own fame tests. The segment is a thoughtful, wary hour on belief's dark gravity, and on the warning signs that a group wants more than your agreement.
quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-margue:
Quotes and Images from the Memoirs of Marguerite de Valois draws on the memoirs of Marguerite, Queen of Navarre, sister and wife of kings in the French wars of religion. David Widger's selection sets her sentences in alphabetical order, each a small lesson from a dangerous court.

Adversity is solitary, she writes, while prosperity dwells in a crowd, and honours and success are followed by envy. Hearsay is liable to the sway of ignorance or malice, mistrust is the sure forerunner of hatred, and much is forgiven to a king. Her own candor shows in the line that she would have praised a correspondent more had he praised her less.
say-fellows-fifty-practical-talks-with-b: Wade C. Smith, author of The Little Jetts Telling Bible Stories, wrote Say, Fellows, fifty practical talks with boys on life's big issues, issued in 1921 by Fleming H. Revell in New York, Chicago, London, and Edinburgh. The talks were adapted from the author's weekly Sunday school lesson treatments in The Sunday School Times, by permission of the editors. Smith gives the book to his mother, whose instruction and example first inspired the purposes and ideals that make for patience, courage, endurance, and faith.
seventy-five-receipts-for-pastry-cakes-a:
Miss Leslie of Philadelphia published these seventy-five receipts for pastry, cakes, and sweetmeats in 1832. A preface states that the receipts are her own, tested by her and her friends with steady success. Each receipt lists its parts and amounts at its head before the method begins.

Leslie writes plainly enough for servants and cooks of modest training. She notes that English and French cookbooks often fail in American kitchens, where fuel, fireplaces, and tools differ. Her book stands as an early American cookbook that trusts home testing over foreign fashion, and it helped shape a national style of baking.
shakespeare-his-life-art-and-characters-:
Rev. H. N. Hudson prepared this fourth, revised edition of his Shakespeare study, entered for copyright in 1872 and issued by Ginn. Hudson inscribed the volumes to Joseph Burnett of Southborough, Massachusetts, on January 1, 1872, after a friendship of more than twenty-five years. Volume one holds the life and a history of English drama.

Contents move from Shakespeare's life to the origin and growth of drama in England, opening with miracle plays. Hudson treats the plays as art and the man as a character worth close study. Generations of American students met Shakespeare first through Hudson's earnest, learned pages.
squash-tennis:
Richard C. Squires wrote Squash Tennis. He lived from 1931 to 2003. The book cost one dollar and dates to March 1968. Richard Kaiser supplied the drawings. The contents name who can play. Plans of play and base strokes follow. Shot-making and the past of the game stand there. Court measures, gear, and the official rules close the list.

Any fan of racquet games with good reflexes will love it, Squires says. The game lacks the staying test of squash racquets. It gives hard-hit strokes in its place. Split-second racquet work thrills the player. The ball comes to you more often here. The test is to read the wide angles. A fast green ball may bounce off five walls. Young players get speed tests from it. Older players get placement and guile. The faster ball grants them more time.
tanakh-jps-1917-genesis:
Genesis, first book of the Torah, opens the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 English Bible, rendered from the Masoretic Text. Its first words tell how God made heaven and earth out of a dark, unformed void, calling light into being first.

Day by day the world takes shape: sky, seas, dry land, plants, sun and moon, birds and beasts. On the sixth day man is made in God's image and blessed to fill the earth, and the seventh day is set apart for rest. Chapter two then shows Eden, its garden, its tree of knowledge, and four great rivers. Readers get the Bible's root tales of making, blessing, and the first human home.
thais:
Anatole France wrote Thais, a novel rendered here by Robert B. Douglas in three parts called The Lotus, The Papyrus, and The Euphorbia, with a banquet scene set within the second part.

The tale opens in the Egyptian desert, where many hermits live in huts of branches and clay along both banks of the Nile. Some live alone yet near enough to aid each other, while others share monastery cells and meet to enjoy their solitude. All eat only after sunset, taking bread with salt and hyssop, and spend their days in prayer and psalms. Readers then meet the monk Paphnutius and the actress Thais, whose fates cross in France's famed tale of faith and desire.
the-art-of-lawn-tennis: Only a Project Gutenberg header is present here, and no pages of the book itself follow it. The header names the work as The Art of Lawn Tennis, by William T. Tilden, 2d, and gives the file as etext number 1451, dated September 1998. It also notes that Charles Keller scanned the text with OmniPage Professional OCR software. the-bible-douay-rheims-book-03-leviticus:
Leviticus, in the Douay-Rheims version, made from the Latin Vulgate and reworked by Bishop Richard Challoner between 1749 and 1752. Behind it stand a Rheims New Testament of 1582 and a Douay Old Testament of 1609 and 1610. No long introduction is shown; the text moves quickly to God speaking from the tabernacle of testimony.

Moses is told to speak to the children of Israel about offerings. A man who offers cattle must bring victims from oxen or sheep. If the offering is a holocaust from the herd, rules follow for what may be brought. Law about sacrifice, given in direct speech, fills the opening chapter. The book's concern is worship in detail: who offers, what is offered, and how it must be done.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-43-zacharias:
Zacharias, in Douay-Rheims translation, worked from the Latin Vulgate and later put through Bishop Richard Challoner's hands in 1749 to 1752. The older printings were a Douay Old Testament (1609, 1610) and a Rheims New Testament (1582). An introduction ties his start to Aggeus, in that same year and on that same occasion. Hidden figures fill his book, the introduction adds, along with promised blessings.

Some promises relate to the synagogue, others to the church of Christ, the introduction adds. Chapter one, dated to the second year of Darius, urges the people to return to God. The Lord, it says, has been very angry with their fathers. Visions follow, meant to give hope of better times after exile.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-55-galatians:
Galatians, in a form of Douay-Rheims translated from Latin Vulgate wording and revised by Bishop Richard Challoner, 1749 to 1752. Behind the wording stand printings at Douay in 1609 and 1610 and at Rheims in 1582. An introduction says its matter is much the same as Romans and dates it to Ephesus, about twenty-three years after the Ascension.

Chapter one blames the Galatians for letting new teachers impose on them, then turns to Paul's own calling. Paul insists he is an apostle not from men, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead. Urgency marks the opening: no long greeting of praise, but a defence of the gospel he first preached to them.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-56-ephesians:
Ephesians, in Douay-Rheims translation, worked from the Latin Vulgate and later put through Bishop Richard Challoner's hands in 1749 to 1752. The older printings were a Douay Old Testament (1609, 1610) and a Rheims New Testament (1582). An introduction warns readers that its matters of faith are very sublime and hard to understand. It dates the letter to about twenty-nine years after the Ascension.

Paul also warns the Ephesians and nearby cities against clever philosophers and false teachers newly come among them. Chapter one gives thanks for blessings received through Christ and calls him head of the whole church. Blessing, election, and a cosmic role for Christ fill the opening lines of a letter more meditative than argumentative in tone.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-61-1-timothy:
First Timothy, in a Douay-Rheims rendering from the Latin Vulgate, in Bishop Richard Challoner's revision of 1749 to 1752. Its New Testament line goes back to Rheims in 1582, its Old Testament line to Douay in 1609 and 1610. An introduction admits uncertainty about where it was written, though a general opinion places it in Macedonia.

Chapter one reminds Timothy of the charge laid on him. Paul also blesses God for mercy he himself received, a theme the heading stresses. Paul writes as an apostle by the commandment of God and Christ Jesus. Counsel to a young church leader fills the letter: teaching, prayer, and order in the household of faith are its stated concerns from the start.
the-chronicles-of-clovis:
Saki, the pen name of H. H. Munro, gathered these short tales under the name Clovis, with an introduction by A. A. Milne. Munro dedicates the book, with reluctantly given consent, to the Lynx Kitten, and dates the dedication August 1911. Clovis, his cool young hero, moves through the stories as a voice of polished mischief.

Milne's introduction sorts books into two classes. Some good things we want to share with the world, and some we want to keep to ourselves, like the secret of a favorite restaurant. Saki's books, for Milne, sat in the second class, guarded from all but a few intimates. He recalls finding Saki in the Westminster Gazette almost as soon as the writer could be found. He bids readers spare a moment, and a tear, for those golden days of the early nineteen hundreds. The tribute sets the tales' tone: brief, elegant, and quietly savage.
the-darwinian-hypothesis:
Thomas H. Huxley heads his essay The Darwinian Hypothesis with a second title, Darwin on the Origin of Species. He begins with the growing vastness of science: beyond the results it harvests, its attempts carry an expanding force that lifts us out of ourselves and transfigures our brief lives.

Measured against the work of nature, he writes, the windy ways of men are but dust that rises and is lightly laid again. Readers must expect new views of the planet's history and of the relations among its creatures, and must not take alarm when a theory as vast as it is novel arrives. A hypothesis built with such skill, he argues, may stand or fall later. Its worth must be tried by the tests of science alone, as befits the heirs of Bacon and the acquitters of Galileo.
the-deputy-of-arcis:
Honore de Balzac's The Deputy of Arcis, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley, opens with Part I, The Election, under the head All Elections Begin with a Bustle. Balzac warns readers first that the town of Arcis-sur-Aube was not the true stage of the events. The district of Arcis votes at Bar-sur-Aube, forty miles off, so no deputy of Arcis sits in the Chamber.

The frame, he admits, dresses one town's facts in another town's setting, a device used more than once in the Comedy of Human Life. Toward the end of April 1839, at ten in the morning, the salon of Madame Marion, widow of a former receiver-general of the Aube. The salon stands stripped of furniture but for curtains, fireplace ornaments, chandelier, and tea-table. Its Aubusson carpet is rolled across the portico steps: a domestic omen of the elections about to cover France.
the-fourth-dimensional-reaches-of-the-ex:
Cora Lenore Williams wrote this essay on the fourth dimension and the Panama-Pacific Fair at San Francisco, printed in 1915. She had written a book called As If and essays on involution.

The contents join a fourteenth-century legend to a study of the fair's courts and palaces. Pictures show the Court of Four Seasons, the Palace of Fine Arts, and the Court of Ages as scenes of odd space. A list of books and poems with fourth-dimensional sight closes the work. Williams reads the fair's grand courts as hints of a world past the three dimensions men can see.
the-great-events-by-famous-historians-vo: Rossiter Johnson was editor-in-chief of The Great Events by Famous Historians. This record is Volume II. the-great-stone-of-sardis: Frank R. Stockton wrote The Great Stone of Sardis. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list. the-history-of-pendennis: William Makepeace Thackeray wrote The History of Pendennis, subtitled his fortunes and misfortunes, his friends and his greatest enemy. the-idol-of-paris: Sarah Bernhardt wrote this novel. An English edition appeared in 1921. Only the title page and contents are present here. The story itself does not appear. She leaves the capital's stage world. Belgium and rural life follow. The chapters bear numbers only, no titles. Nothing more of the plot can be read here.
the-life-of-venerable-sister-margaret-bo:
A sister of Cedar Rapids, Iowa, translated the life of Venerable Sister Margaret Bourgeois from the French and signs herself only as a religieuse. Her preface says an 1818 French edition charmed her into the work. No English version existed in the United States, she believed.

Translation sheets gathered over years of stops and starts at last reached print. She timed the book to the second centennial of Bourgeois arrival in America. Bourgeois founded the Congregation of Notre Dame at Montreal in 1659, as the title page states, and taught children in a stable school there.
the-metropolis:
Upton Sinclair published The Metropolis in 1908, a novel of New York wealth in twenty-one chapters. Chapter One opens at a quiet uptown hotel, where a general tells his chauffeur to return at ten-thirty. His companion, Montague, gazes around the corridor trembling a little with anticipation. The marble columns and gilded carvings are not what move him, Sinclair says. Montague thinks instead of the men he is about to meet.

Fresh from the country, Montague has crowded a great deal into one day. First came the vision of the whirling, seething city, the centre of all his hopes for the future. Now the evening promises introductions to the powerful men who run that city. Sinclair positions his newcomer at the threshold of the moneyed world he will anatomize. The novel begins as an entrance into high finance's drawing rooms.
the-outdoor-chums-on-the-gulf-or-rescuin:
Captain Quincy Allen published The Outdoor Chums on the Gulf, or Rescuing the Lost Balloonists, in 1911. The contents list twenty-five chapters, ending with The Secret of the Sealed Packet. Chapter One, Under Sealed Orders, opens at Frank's house, where the boys press him to keep his word and tell his news.

The chapter titles promise a southern trip: Caught in a Fire Trap, Headed South, The Swamp Fugitive, a Florida sheriff, a motor boat breakdown, and Bluff's first alligator. A message from the air and a dash upon the Gulf build toward the rescue named in the subtitle. The boys' club tours with rod, gun, and camera.
the-passenger-from-calais:
Arthur Griffiths wrote The Passenger from Calais, a mystery first printed in January 1906 and reprinted three times by 1908. The tale is told by Colonel Annesley. His crossing from Dover to Calais was rough, with drizzle, and few passengers landed on that Sunday in late July. He expected a crowded train to Central Europe.

At the siding, the Lucerne sleeping car of the Engadine express stood waiting. Annesley found he was not merely the first passenger but the only one. His place was booked through, and the empty train de luxe sets an odd, quiet opening for a railway mystery by the author of The Rome Express.
the-rock-of-chickamauga-a-story-of-the-w: Joseph A. the-sun-of-quebec-a-story-of-a-great-cri: Joseph A. Altsheler, author of Lords of the Wild, wrote this story of a great crisis in his French and Indian War series, copyrighted by D. the-world-english-bible-web-genesis:
Genesis stands alone here as book one of the World English Bible. Its first verse has God creating the heavens and the earth. Darkness covers a formless, empty world. God's Spirit hovers over the surface of the waters. Light appears at God's command. God sees the light is good and separates it from darkness.

Day and Night receive their names on that first day. An expanse then divides waters above from waters below. A footnote explains a Hebrew grammatical marker in the first verse. Numbered verses make the creation account easy to follow. From Eden to Joseph, Genesis lays the Bible's foundation stories.
types-of-naval-officers-drawn-from-the-h: A. T. Mahan's Types of Naval Officers, drawn from the history of the British Navy, was issued at London in 1902. Mahan had written the Influence of Sea Power upon History and lives of Nelson and Farragut. The contents open with an introductory chapter on naval warfare at the start of the eighteenth century. Only the title page and start of the contents are present here, so Mahan's studies themselves do not appear.
venus-and-adonis:
William Shakespeare dedicated Venus and Adonis to Henry Wriothesley, Earl of Southampton, and called the poem the first heir of his invention. His letter of dedication fears the world will blame him for resting so weak a burden on so strong a prop. He vows to use his idle hours on graver work if this piece finds favor, and to leave off if it proves deformed.

The poem itself opens at dawn. As the sun takes leave of the weeping morning, rose-cheeked Adonis rides out to the chase, a youth who loves hunting and laughs love to scorn. Venus, sick with longing, hurries to him and woos him boldly, calling him fairer than herself and the chief flower of the field. Shakespeare builds the whole poem on that chase reversed: the goddess hunts the boy, and the boy wants none of her.
vocal-mastery-talks-with-master-singers-: Harriette Brower, author of Piano Mastery, gathered Vocal Mastery from talks with master singers and teachers. Frederick A. Stokes Company issued it at New York in 1920. Pages present here hold the title page and the start of the contents, so the talks themselves are not shown. Contents promise Enrico Caruso on the value of work. Geraldine Farrar speaks on the will to succeed, and Victor Maurel on mind as everything. A visit to Lilli Lehmann follows. Amelita Galli-Curci treats self-teaching, and Giuseppe De Luca treats ceaseless effort.
within-the-temple-of-isis:
Belle M. Wagner published this occult novel in Denver in 1899. She dedicated it to her husband, Henry Wagner, a doctor. The publisher's preface calls the story unique. It says no other book in print matches it. The preface links the tale to ancient Egypt and to priests of Isis who knew nature's hidden workings.

Those priests, called hierophants, are said to enter the temple and see mysteries behind a veil. The preface claims wise people can still do the same today. Readers get a story framed as secret knowledge, not plain history. Faith, mystery, and hidden power drive its appeal.
wonderful-balloon-ascents-or-the-conques:
F. Marion wrote this 1870 history of balloons and balloon voyages. His preface opens with a stone honouring Vincent Lunardi, the first aerial traveller in Britain. He flew from London in September 1784 and stayed aloft over two hours. Marion says no modern discovery stirred more hope than the balloon. The Montgolfier brothers get chief credit for it.

Marion also notes a puzzle. The balloon reached full form at birth and barely changed in ninety years. Coxwell and Glaisher flew much the same craft that amazed Paris in 1783. Readers get pioneer flights, famous aeronauts, and the dream of ruling the skies.
